title: Understanding the Risks of Public AWS AMIs: Hidden Dangers of Malicious and Misconfigured Images
description: Key Takeaways Public Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) speed up deployment, but anyone can publish one, so they should never be trusted based on their name or description alone. Malicious or misconfigured AMIs can carry vulnerable software, embedded malware, exposed credentials, or insecure configurations that compromise workloads as soon as they launch. The whoAMI attack, disclosed […]
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Public Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) speed up deployment, but anyone can publish one, so they should never be trusted based on their name or description alone.
  • Malicious or misconfigured AMIs can carry vulnerable software, embedded malware, exposed credentials, or insecure configurations that compromise workloads as soon as they launch.
  • The whoAMI attack, disclosed by Datadog Security Labs, shows how attackers can publish look-alike images that get picked up by pipelines that don’t verify the AMI owner.
  • A single compromised source image can spread through Golden AMIs to every account, region, and workload built from it, and images that aren’t rebuilt regularly drift out of date.
  • Validating image owners, rebuilding Golden AMIs regularly, using AWS Allowed AMIs, and continuously monitoring with Qualys TotalCloud help keep malicious and misconfigured images out of production.

Introduction

A developer or CI/CD pipeline searches for an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) using a familiar image name. If the workflow does not verify the image’s owner, it may select a malicious image that resembles a trusted one. This is the risk highlighted by Datadog Security Labs’ whoAMI research: an image-selection mistake can introduce a supply chain compromise before an application even starts running.

The impact extends beyond image selection. Malicious or misconfigured AMIs can introduce vulnerable software, embedded malware, exposed credentials, or insecure configurations into newly launched EC2 instances. When such images are incorporated into Golden AMI workflows and reused across environments, the resulting risks can propagate to multiple workloads.

Securing AMIs therefore requires more than checking a few cloud configuration settings. Organizations need to validate image provenance, assess image contents before deployment, secure infrastructure automation, and monitor workloads for signs of compromise.

This article examines the risks associated with public and misconfigured AMIs, analyzes relevant attack scenarios, maps supported behaviors to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and explores how AWS security controls and Qualys capabilities can help reduce risk throughout the AMI lifecycle.

AMIs Provide the Foundation for EC2 Deployments

An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is a template used to launch Amazon EC2 instances. It includes the operating system, installed software, configuration, and storage mappings needed to create an instance.

AMIs can be private or public:

Private AMIs are shared with authorized AWS accounts and are commonly used to maintain standardized, organization-approved images.

Public AMIs are available to AWS customers in the region where they are shared. They allow organizations to reuse community- or vendor-provided images, reducing the effort required to prepare new EC2 instances.

Security Risks of Public AMIs

Using public AMIs introduces multiple security risks because organizations rely on third-party-maintained software and configurations.

The primary risks include:

  • Outdated operating systems and vulnerable software packages
  • Embedded malware or cryptominers
  • Hardcoded credentials or sensitive configuration files
  • Accidental publication of internal AMIs
  • Image impersonation through misleading names or descriptions
  • Supply chain compromise through insecure Golden AMIs

Although these risks differ in execution, they all originate from inadequate validation of image provenance and insufficient governance throughout the AMI lifecycle.

Attack Analysis

1. Malicious Public AMIs

Public AMIs published by unknown or untrusted users can intentionally contain malicious components designed to compromise workloads immediately after deployment.

Embedded Malware

Attackers may embed malware directly into an AMI before publishing it. Once an EC2 instance is launched, malicious payloads execute automatically, allowing attackers to establish persistence, communicate with command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, deploy ransomware, or mine cryptocurrency.

Vulnerable or Weaponized Software

Instead of embedding malware directly, attackers may intentionally distribute images containing outdated software with known vulnerabilities. Once deployed, these vulnerabilities can be exploited remotely to gain unauthorized access or to escalate privileges.

Image Impersonation (whoAMI Attack)

Datadog Security Labs disclosed the whoAMI attack, in which attackers publish malicious AMIs with names that closely resemble trusted vendor images.

If developers or automation pipelines search for AMIs by image name alone, without validating the image owner, a malicious image may be selected and deployed instead of the legitimate one.

This attack demonstrates that image metadata can serve as an effective attack vector even when the infrastructure code remains unchanged.

2. Misconfigured AMIs Can Introduce Inherited Security Weaknesses

An AMI need not be intentionally malicious to pose security risks. Images containing outdated software, exposed secrets, or insecure system settings can carry these weaknesses into newly launched EC2 instances.

Common examples include:

  • Unpatched operating systems and software packages
  • Hardcoded credentials or sensitive configuration files
  • Embedded SSH private keys
  • Insecure SSH authentication settings
  • Unnecessary services or insecure system configurations

These weaknesses can increase the attack surface of instances launched from the image. Depending on the configuration and surrounding security controls, they may expose workloads to unauthorized access, credential compromise, or exploitation of known vulnerabilities.

Security risks can also arise during deployment. For example, attaching an overly permissive IAM role to an EC2 instance can grant compromised workloads access to cloud resources beyond what they require. Similarly, accidentally sharing an internal AMI can expose an image to unauthorized parties.

3. Supply Chain Risks from Golden AMIs

Golden AMIs provide a standardized and secure baseline for enterprise deployments. However, if the source image is compromised, all derived images inherit the same vulnerabilities.

For example, if an organization creates a Golden AMI from:

  • an untrusted public AMI,
  • a vulnerable marketplace image, or
  • an internally compromised image,

Every EC2 instance launched from that Golden AMI inherits the same weaknesses.

This significantly amplifies the impact of a single compromised image by propagating vulnerabilities across multiple AWS accounts, regions, and production environments.

Version Drift

Even well-maintained Golden AMIs become outdated if they are not rebuilt regularly.

Organizations often patch running instances while continuing to deploy new workloads from older images. This creates inconsistent security baselines, leaving newly launched systems vulnerable to already-patched CVEs.

AMI Inventory and Lineage Challenges

Large enterprises frequently maintain hundreds of AMIs across multiple AWS accounts and Regions.

Without centralized inventory and lineage tracking, security teams struggle to determine:

  • which workloads originated from vulnerable images,
  • which Golden AMIs inherited vulnerabilities,
  • which production systems require immediate remediation.

Maintaining complete image lineage significantly improves incident response and vulnerability management.

MITRE ATT&CK Mapping

The following ATT&CK techniques represent behaviors that may occur across the AMI attack scenarios discussed in this article. Not every technique is necessarily present in every attack.

End-to-End Attack Scenario

A realistic attack chain may unfold as follows:

  1. An attacker publishes a malicious public AMI using a trusted-looking name.
  2. A developer or CI/CD pipeline searches for an image without validating the owner.
  3. The malicious image is selected and used to create an internal Golden AMI.
  4. The Golden AMI is replicated across multiple AWS accounts and Regions.
  5. New EC2 instances inherit the malicious software or insecure configurations.
  6. Malware establishes persistence and communicates with attacker-controlled infrastructure.
  7. Attackers steal credentials, escalate privileges, move laterally, and compromise additional cloud resources.

Potential Impact

Deploying a malicious or misconfigured AMI can lead to:

  • Unauthorized access to EC2 instances
  • Credential theft
  • Data exfiltration
  • Cryptocurrency mining
  • Increased cloud costs
  • Lateral movement across AWS resources
  • Supply chain compromise
  • Regulatory and compliance violations
  • Reputational damage

Mitigation and Best Practices

Preventive Controls

Organizations should prevent vulnerable AMIs from entering production by implementing strong governance controls.

Recommended practices include:

  • Assess AMIs for vulnerabilities before deployment using services such as Amazon Inspector or Qualys TotalCloud AMI Scan.
  • Build and regularly rebuild Golden AMIs through CI/CD pipelines.

Automate Golden AMI creation and validation through CI/CD pipelines, incorporating the latest operating system patches, security updates, and hardened configurations before images are approved and distributed. Periodically rebuild and retire outdated images to prevent version drift, which can cause newly launched EC2 instances to inherit unpatched software, known vulnerabilities, or deprecated security configurations. This helps maintain consistent security baselines across deployments.

  • Validate image provenance by verifying publisher identity and AMI owner IDs.

Always define the AMI owner ID to prevent name confusion attacks.

AWS warning when omitting owners:

  • Restrict public sharing of internally created AMIs.

Avoid making AMIs public unless necessary and ensure all sensitive data is removed beforehand.

  • Use AWS Allowed AMIs to enforce trusted image sources.

Utilize AWS’s Allowed AMIs feature to enforce trust boundaries and restrict instance launches to vetted image sources.

The core configuration for Allowed AMIs is the ImageCriteria configuration that defines the criteria for allowed AMIs. The following JSON structure shows the parameters that can be specified:

  • Treat AMIs as third-party software dependencies that require security review before approval.

Detective Controls

Continuous monitoring is equally important.

Organizations should:

  • Monitor AWS CloudTrail for AMI creation, modification, sharing, and launch events.
  • Detect EC2 instances launched from unknown or unapproved AMIs.
  • Alert when AMIs become publicly accessible.
  • Monitor image usage across AWS accounts.
  • Enable drift detection for Golden AMIs.
  • Continuously scan deployed workloads for inherited vulnerabilities.

Governance and Lifecycle Management

Effective AMI governance extends beyond deployment.

Organizations should:

  • Maintain a centralized inventory of approved AMIs.
  • Track AMI lineage to understand parent-child image relationships.
  • Periodically review sharing permissions.
  • Remove obsolete or unused AMIs.
  • Integrate AMI validation into change management and deployment workflows.

Securing the AWS AMI Lifecycle with Qualys

Securing AMIs requires visibility and protection across multiple stages of the cloud deployment lifecycle. Organizations must assess images before deployment, identify infrastructure misconfigurations, monitor deployed workloads, and respond to potential threats.

Qualys provides capabilities across these stages through its TotalCloud CNAPP platform and complementary vulnerability management and endpoint security solutions.

1. Assess AMIs Before Deployment

Qualys TotalCloud provides an AMI Scan capability that uses snapshot-based scanning to assess Amazon Machine Images before deployment, without requiring an EC2 instance to be launched or an agent to be installed.

The assessment helps identify operating system vulnerabilities, missing patches, outdated software components, and configuration issues within AMIs.

Integrating AMI scanning into image-building and Golden AMI promotion workflows allows security teams to assess images before they are approved for production use. This helps reduce the likelihood of deploying images containing known security weaknesses.

However, vulnerability assessment alone does not establish the authenticity of an AMI publisher or guarantee that an image is free from malicious code. Organizations should continue to validate AMI ownership and publisher information using AWS-native controls.

2. Identify Infrastructure Misconfigurations Before Deployment

Qualys Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Security helps identify security misconfigurations in supported infrastructure templates before resources are deployed.

By integrating IaC scanning into CI/CD workflows, development and security teams can identify insecure infrastructure definitions in Terraform and AWS CloudFormation templates before they reach production.

This complements AMI scanning by assessing the infrastructure deployment process, helping organizations identify configuration weaknesses that could expose EC2 workloads.

3. Strengthen Cloud Posture and Workload Security

Qualys TotalCloud combines Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM), Cloud Workload Protection (CWP), and Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (CIEM) capabilities to provide visibility into cloud security risks.

These capabilities help organizations:

  • Identify cloud misconfigurations, including relevant AMI exposure, encryption, and launch-permission issues.
  • Assess vulnerabilities across supported cloud workloads and prioritize remediation based on risk.
  • Identify excessive cloud permissions and risky identity relationships that could increase the impact of a compromised workload.

This helps security teams understand not only the security state of an AMI, but also the configuration and identity risks associated with the EC2 instances launched from it.

4. Remediate Vulnerabilities and Automate Security Workflows

Identifying vulnerabilities is only one part of securing the AMI lifecycle. Organizations must also ensure that identified weaknesses are addressed across running workloads and future image builds.

Qualys Vulnerability Management, Detection and Response (VMDR) helps identify and prioritize vulnerabilities across supported assets. Qualys Patch Management can support deploying applicable security patches to supported running workloads.

Qualys Flow and TotalCloud workflow automation capabilities can further help operationalize security findings through customized remediation workflows, incident routing, and supported integrations.

For Golden AMI environments, organizations should incorporate remediation into their image-building pipelines and periodically rebuild approved images to ensure that future deployments inherit updated security baselines.

Extending Image Security Across Multi-Cloud Environments

Although this article focuses on AWS AMIs, similar risks exist across cloud platforms wherever organizations use reusable machine images to provision workloads. Azure and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), for example, provide image services that allow teams to create, share, and reuse standardized images across their environments.

The terminology and image-sharing mechanisms differ across providers, but the underlying security concerns remain similar: an image may contain outdated software, insecure configurations, or embedded sensitive information, while insufficient governance can expose internally maintained images or allow untrusted images to enter deployment workflows.

Across these platforms, organizations should maintain visibility into image metadata and apply consistent governance practices. This includes identifying image owners and sources, restricting access to approved images, reviewing sharing permissions, assessing image contents for vulnerabilities and exposed secrets, and periodically retiring outdated images.

For organizations operating in multi-cloud environments, centralized cloud security monitoring can help identify configuration weaknesses and exposure to vulnerabilities across image-related resources and the workloads launched from them. Qualys capabilities such as cloud posture assessment, image vulnerability scanning, infrastructure-as-code security, and workload protection can contribute to this broader security approach, subject to the supported cloud services and product configurations.

Treating machine images as part of the software supply chain, rather than simply as infrastructure artifacts, helps organizations apply consistent security governance from image creation through deployment and ongoing workload operation.

Conclusion

Public AMIs provide significant operational benefits, but they should never be trusted by default. As cloud-native deployments become increasingly automated, AMIs have become critical components of the software supply chain whose integrity directly affects the security of downstream workloads.

Securing the AMI lifecycle requires organizations to validate image sources, assess images for vulnerabilities before deployment, maintain governed Golden AMI workflows, and continuously monitor the workloads launched from them. AWS-native capabilities such as Allowed AMIs help restrict image usage to approved sources, while security solutions such as Qualys TotalCloud help identify image vulnerabilities, cloud misconfigurations, and risks across deployed workloads.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

What is the whoAMI attack?

Attackers publish malicious AMIs with names that resemble trusted vendor images. Pipelines that search by name and do not verify the owner can select the malicious image.

Is a public AMI safe if the name looks official?

No. Anyone can publish a public AMI. Trust comes from the owner ID and publisher, not the name or description.

What does Qualys TotalCloud AMI Scan check?

It uses snapshot-based scanning to assess an AMI before deployment, without launching an instance or installing an agent. It helps find operating system vulnerabilities, missing patches, outdated software, and configuration issues.

Does AMI Scan prove the image is not malicious?

No. It does not establish publisher authenticity or guarantee an image is free of malicious code. Validate ownership with AWS controls, including Allowed AMIs and owner ID.

Why rebuild Golden AMIs?

Patching running instances does not update the image. New launches from an old Golden AMI inherit already-patched CVEs. Rebuild and retire outdated images on a schedule.

fullContent:
LOS ANGELES—Calling the experience deeply unsettling and admitting they could not find any rational explanation for what they had just witnessed on live television, basketball viewers around the country told reporters Thursday they were profoundly disturbed after spotting Jack Nicholson sitting courtside at eight simultaneous NBA games. “I saw Nicholson eating a hot dog next to Owen Wilson at the Lakers game and obviously thought nothing of it, but then I flipped over to Knicks-Warriors and he was there too, eating a cheesesteak next to Spike Lee, and my stomach just dropped,” said NBA fan Brendan Carroll, echoing the unease of countless viewers who frantically flooded social media with screenshots of the acclaimed actor grinning onscreen at concurrent basketball games in Los Angeles, Detroit, Orlando, Indianapolis, New York, Miami, Memphis, and San Antonio, seemingly in violation of the basic laws that govern the universe. “I kept switching channels to see if it was some weird editing trick or tape delay, but no—he’s clearly present in real time at each of those games. When they showed him at the Pacers game, I swear he looked straight into the camera and put a finger to his lips. It made chills go up my spine. I love the guy as an actor, but there is something seriously wrong about this.” Reached for comment, Nicholson told reporters that he, too, was unnerved by his presence on eight different broadcasts, as he’d been at home all night watching the Lakers game on TV.

The post Visa and Mastercard Urge Federal Judge To Approve $38,000,000,000 Swipe Fee Settlement appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
Merchants could soon pay lower card fees and gain the right to refuse certain credit cards under a $38 billion settlement now before a federal judge.

Visa and Mastercard urged a judge on Monday to approve the deal, reports Reuters.

The agreement would end claims that the card networks charged merchants excessive fees to process credit card payments.

The settlement would cut the average swipe fee by 0.1 percentage point for five years and cap fees on standard consumer cards at 1.25% for eight years.

It would also end the Honor All Cards rule, which requires merchants to accept all Visa and Mastercard cards or none.

Merchants could instead choose whether to accept commercial cards, premium consumer cards or standard consumer cards.

Visa says the deal would also give merchants more options to surcharge and add a new merchant education program.

Visa’s lawyer Michael Shuster says that the settlement provides “potent” relief for merchants, while the card network is not “jumping with joy.”

“It’s going to change life for the [card] networks.”

U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan in Brooklyn did not rule at the hearing, but said rejecting the settlement could lead to a protracted process in the 21-year-old case.

Cogan granted preliminary approval in June, and a different judge rejected an earlier $30 billion version in 2024.

The post XRP ETF Is Down $216M as Ripple Token Falls 35%: Can The Price Recover to $1.71? appeared first on 99Bitcoins.
fullContent:
Franklin Templeton’s spot XRP fund, which buys and holds the coin itself, disclosed on November 13 that it held 293.1 million Ripple XRP tokens at the end of September, worth $440 million. That was already $62 million below what the fund paid for them, and XRP has fallen another 35% since.

The numbers come from the quarterly report of the Franklin XRP ETF, which trades under the ticker XRPZ. They show the fund kept growing through the summer even as the price slid.

We divided the fund’s cost by the tokens it held. The fund paid an average of about $1.71 per XRP. XRP last closed above that price on January 30. At today’s $0.974, the September stake sits about $216 million underwater. XRP needs a 76% rally to get the fund back to even.

That loss is on paper only. The fund hasn’t sold any XRP, and no investor has pulled money out.

Market Cap

Franklin’s Ripple XRP Fund Grew 30% in the Third Quarter

The fund’s quarterly report to the SEC covers July through September. Its Ripple XRP holdings rose from 225.37 million on July 1 to 293.11 million on September 30, up 30%.

  • New money: 26.6 million XRP was bought with cash from new shares, and 41.25 million came in as tokens handed over directly by investors.
  • No exits: the fund had no redemptions in the quarter. It sold 108,834 XRP, only to pay its 0.19% yearly fee.
  • Shares: 27 million shares outstanding at a net asset value of $16.28 each, almost double the 14.7 million shares at the end of March.
  • Custody: Coinbase Custody holds the tokens.

The fund has kept adding since. Franklin’s fund page listed 314.77 million XRP on November 13, about 21.7 million more than at the end of September. Those tokens were bought much cheaper, so they lower the fund’s average cost a little.

DISCOVER: 20+ Next Crypto to Explode in 2026

XRP Hasn’t Traded Above the Fund’s $1.71 Cost Since January

The report puts the fund’s cost at $501.43 million for 293.11 million XRP. That works out to about $1.71 per token. The fund launched on November 24, 2025, with XRP above $2.20, and most of its early buying happened before February’s drop.

  • On September 30: XRP at $1.50 left the stake worth $439.7 million, 12.3% below cost.
  • Today: at $0.974, the same 293.1 million XRP is worth about $285 million, roughly $216 million (43%) below cost.
  • To break even: XRP must climb back to about $1.71, a 76% rally from here.

The fund isn’t alone. All U.S. spot XRP ETFs held about $1.16 billion last week, down from $1.51 billion in late October. Between November 9 and 13, they lost about $36 million to net outflows. Fewer new buyers mean less cheap Ripple XRP to pull these funds’ average cost down.

DISCOVER: XRP Price Falls 22% Since Garlinghouse’s “Never Give Up” Pledge: What Is Ripple’s Plan?

Ripple XRP Price Analysis: $1.05 Is the Line to Reclaim

Ripple XRP trades at $0.974 on Binance after falling below $1 on November 13 for the first time since August. On the daily chart, it sits below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $1.218, and its 200-day EMA at $1.326.

  • Resistance: $1.05, which held as a floor four times between June and August: on June 6, July 13, July 28, and August 1. Above that, $1.26, a floor that held five times between February and October before it broke this month.
  • Support: $0.893, last weekend’s low. XRP tested it on Saturday and again on Sunday, so it has only two touches so far. It is the year’s low. Below it, the next marked level is $0.633, the top of XRP’s 2024 range.

XRPUSDT 1D chart. Source: TradingView

Path What has to happen Next stop
Recovery A daily close above $1.05 $1.26, the February-October floor
Range Holding between $0.893 and $1.05 Sideways trading under $1
Breakdown A daily close below $0.893 $0.633, the 2024 range top

The fund’s next quarterly report will show whether its investors kept buying through November’s slide. Until Ripple XRP gets back above $1.05, the fund stays far below its $1.71 cost.

title: Coinbase Brings User-Approved Trading Into ChatGPT
description:
Key Takeaways Every plugin order needs a confirmation card. A confirmed order can still sit unfilled. Agent futures trading uses […]
The post Coinbase Brings User-Approved Trading Into ChatGPT appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Every plugin order needs a confirmation card.
  • A confirmed order can still sit unfilled.
  • Agent futures trading uses your main portfolio.
  • Auto-stop pauses trading; it doesn’t sell holdings.

Coinbase announced the official plugin on November 17, five months after launching Coinbase for Agents on June 11, the platform that first let AI assistants connect to Coinbase accounts.

Once an account is linked, a user can view the connected portfolio and ask ChatGPT to place, edit or cancel orders. Each of those actions produces a Coinbase confirmation card, and nothing goes to the exchange until the user approves it. The plugin is limited to U.S. customers. Which products a user can trade depends on their Coinbase account eligibility, and access also depends on their ChatGPT account and workspace.

Orders are routed through Coinbase Advanced, and Coinbase’s developer documentation says Advanced Trade fees and eligibility requirements apply. A trade requested in a chat is priced under the same fee schedule as one entered on the exchange directly.

The plugin is not the only way to connect the two services, and the route a user picks decides who makes the final call on each order.

Two ways to put Coinbase inside ChatGPT

Official Coinbase plugin

Setup: Coinbase’s own plugin, linked to the account

Before an order leaves: A confirmation card for every order, edit and cancellation

x402 payments: Not offered

Custom MCP connection

Setup: Added by hand as a custom MCP server; may require ChatGPT developer mode

Before an order leaves: Whatever the user instructs; in Coinbase’s tests, ChatGPT placed clear orders in a single turn

x402 payments: Available

MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, is the standard AI assistants use to call outside tools. x402 is Coinbase’s protocol for software paying for data or services, typically in stablecoins.

Both routes run in the same chat window and describe orders in the same fluent language. What separates them is whether a person approves each order, or whether the original instruction already counts as approval.

The card shows what ChatGPT understood

Take a plain request: “Buy $100 of Bitcoin with a limit order.” It names the asset, the direction, the amount and the order type. It does not say the highest price the user will pay, how long the order should stay open, whether the $100 includes fees or which portfolio should fund it.

Those points have to be settled before a card can appear, either by ChatGPT asking or by defaults filling the gaps. Coinbase’s documentation says assistants reliably build orders “from clear, well-specified instructions”, and the vaguer the request, the more of the order the assistant decides. The lines worth reading on the card are therefore the ones the user never typed: the limit price and the duration.

Approval starts an order; it doesn’t finish one

Tapping approve sends an instruction. Whether anything was bought depends on what happens after Coinbase receives it, and a chat reply can run ahead of the facts. Coinbase’s agent documentation warns that on hosted chat clients, high-reasoning modes have sometimes drafted an order and stopped before executing it, leaving the user to ask again.

An order that does reach the exchange can still sit unfilled. Because the plugin covers stocks as well as crypto, equity rules come with it. Coinbase’s stock-order guidance says limit orders execute only at the set price or better when enough liquidity is available, so they can fill partially or not at all. Stock market orders are limited to regular trading hours, and extended sessions carry their own restrictions.

Partial fills change what a cancellation does. Cancelling a $100 buy after $60 has executed removes the remaining $40. The $60 position stays in the account at whatever price it filled.

When the instruction is the approval

On the custom connection, an agent can act on standing instructions instead of waiting for a tap on each order. Coindoo has examined how far automated execution sits from independent AI decision-making. For a Coinbase user, the more immediate question is which money the agent can reach.

Coinbase’s answer is portfolio scope. Its documentation advises creating a separate portfolio for the agent, funding it only with what the user is prepared to risk and selecting that portfolio on the approval screen. Transfers through the agent connection are limited to moves between the user’s own portfolios, with no withdrawals to outside addresses.

That isolation covers spot crypto only. Coinbase’s U.S. dated futures work only in the default portfolio, so a user who wants an agent to trade them has to add the default portfolio to the agent’s access, and with it everything else that portfolio holds.

READ MORE:

Hyperliquid Nvidia Perp: TradeXYZ Halves Leverage to 10x

Coinbase’s server-side limits and what they leave open

Coinbase added another layer on November 11. Its Agent Controls announcement lets users cap the dollar size of each trade, cap an agent’s total trading over 24 hours and set an auto-stop that pauses the agent once a portfolio falls by a chosen percentage. The limits are enforced on Coinbase’s servers and sit behind the user’s login, so the agent cannot loosen them. Permissions by product type were marked as coming soon.

The two caps stop different failures. A $100 per-trade limit blocks one oversized order but still allows fifty $100 orders in a day. The 24-hour cap is what stops the fiftieth, because trades beyond it are not executed.

Auto-stop is narrower than its name suggests. Coinbase describes it as halting new agent trades until the user switches trading back on. It has not described it as cancelling orders already resting on the book or closing positions, so anything bought before the trigger keeps moving with the market after the agent goes quiet.

A conventional stop order actively tries to exit, but it carries a gap of its own. Coinbase’s U.S. derivatives guidance explains that when a market reopens beyond a stop level, the order can fill at the opening price rather than at the trigger.

Agent Controls arrived six days before the plugin and are described in terms of agents acting on a user’s behalf. For trades placed through the plugin, the control Coinbase has put in front of every order is the confirmation card itself.

Checking the result in Coinbase

After approval, the record that counts sits in Coinbase’s order history, not in ChatGPT’s reply. It shows the order’s status, how much filled, the average price, the fees charged and any quantity still open. A partly filled limit order left open is still a live instruction, and a futures position an agent opened stays in the default portfolio after any auto-stop.

Neither the plugin nor Agent Controls closes a position on the user’s behalf. That still takes an order of its own, approved like every other.

The post Cancer Patient Charged Extra $2,000 To Ring Bell appeared first on The Onion.
fullContent:
TULSA, OK—Stressing that this was the last thing he needed after three months of chemotherapy, local cancer patient Robert Marcinik was reportedly shocked to learn Thursday that he had been charged an extra $2,000 to ring the bell. “I rang the bell to mark the end of my lung cancer treatment, and now I have this surprise bill from my insurance company because apparently it’s not covered,” said Marcinik, adding that the weakness and nausea he had experienced from weeks of chemo paled in comparison to the stomach-churning realization that clanging the bell was considered an adjuvant therapy requiring pre-authorization. “The bell at the hospital is out-of-network, and according to Blue Cross Blue Shield, I should have used the in-network bell 40 miles from here. They said my oncologist should have written a referral to ring the bell, but even if he had, my HMO wouldn’t have covered it. Plus, each pull of the rope is an individual charge—I wish I hadn’t gone hog wild dinging that thing.” At press time, the hospital’s financial services team told Marcinik they were pleased to reduce the price to $1800 if he was willing to pay out-of-pocket.

ZachXBT: Indian CID Froze $3M Gate Over Merlin Bridge Mix-Up
description:
ZachXBT says a Gate Merlin bridge India freeze locked about $3 million after Andhra Pradesh CID mistook Merlin Chain Bitcoin rails for alibarbit.bit pig-butchering proceeds. A Guntur court has now ordered Gate to hand that balance to the complainant. His November 17 analysis finds no theft link on the chain into the frozen account. That […]
The post ZachXBT: Indian CID Froze $3M Gate Over Merlin Bridge Mix-Up appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
ZachXBT says a Gate Merlin bridge India freeze locked about $3 million after Andhra Pradesh CID mistook Merlin Chain Bitcoin rails for alibarbit.bit pig-butchering proceeds. A Guntur court has now ordered Gate to hand that balance to the complainant. His November 17 analysis finds no theft link on the chain into the frozen account.

That is the plain read. A real romance-investment fraud case. A compliance tool that misnamed a Bitcoin Layer 2 bridge. A custodial freeze that treated the wrong hop as the crime.

What Andhra Pradesh CID Said It Solved

Andhra Pradesh CID registered Cr. No. 10/2025 after a Tenali complainant said she lost about Rs 15 crore. That is roughly $1.5 million in the department’s public account. She said fake platforms Honeycombapi.org and Alibarbit.bit took the funds. CID chief Ravishankar Ayyanar told The New Indian Express the team traced 15 Bitcoin transfers to four Gate.io accounts. Assets were frozen through court process. Eight people were charged with help from the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre.

ZachXBT’s timeline puts the alleged May 2025 loss near $1.7 million across BTC, USDT, DOGE, and SOL. A charge sheet followed in March 2026. On October 30, 2026, the VI Additional Junior Civil Judge-cum-Special Court for CID Cases, Guntur, allowed Crl.M.P. No. 298/2026. The order released crypto in Gate UIDs 14531479, 8407150, 7633997, and 119769 toward interim custody for the complainant. It directed Gate Global Corp. to convert those balances into USDT on TRON and send them to a designated victim wallet.

Inspector D. Kasi Viswanadh’s CID notice, published in ZachXBT’s evidence set, told the Gate account holder the coins had passed two non-custodial wallets and exchanges before KYC at Gate.io. It ordered a personal appearance in Mangalagiri within 15 days. It warned that non-cooperation could mean forfeiture to the victim.

What the Gate Merlin Bridge India Freeze Trail Shows

The Gate freeze in India turns on a Merlin bridge labeling error, ZachXBT argues. It is not a fresh theft hop into that account.

User xxxkeym says he deposited 15 BTC to Gate on July 16, 2025. Four days later Gate froze the account and asked for source-of-funds proof. Public Bitcoin data matches the deposit he and ZachXBT cite. Transaction 885f3afab562251b222363cf12095e864ddb94636674b01f0cdb05997e5a54a0 moved about 15 BTC from cold wallet 3NcBhqKnyo8dfzqfG1p5rbaKJFV8yLnx3u into Gate deposit address 17mpajZ6Nq3dG3T6wUhaXxYF4Qy9HJnYx5. ZachXBT says that cold wallet was funded by the user’s own OKX and Binance withdrawals in January 2023. The coins then sat dormant for years. CID never froze those exchange accounts.

The same Gate deposit address later took more 2025 BTC from bc1pkkwqyxn3rm608ryuqg9hyqna0syq4jx5pxkr7pzg8n3usx6tyqfst5u966, also controlled by xxxkeym. Those coins arrived after three Merlin Chain bridge outs totaling about 25 BTC in March, May, and June 2025. Compliance tooling had tagged Merlin payout addresses bc1quzwkggdf6ly06mrrnnled0qdr57w770k45n5n7 and bc1qtu66zfqxj6pam6e0zunwnggh87f5pjr7vdr5cd as alibarbit.bit. ZachXBT says both are Merlin Chain bridge rails. They sit unlabeled in most commercial screening products. A sample payout shows bc1quzw… funding xxxkeym’s taproot wallet for about 10.1367 BTC. That matches Merlin-side withdrawals from contract 0x59fd8E3a….

ZachXBT adds that xxxkeym bridged 50 BTC into Merlin on March 28, 2024. That was more than a year before the alleged May 2025 scam. The three later withdrawals came out of that balance. He reports zero on-chain ties between xxxkeym and the complainant’s theft path. Separately, on July 15, 2025, xxxkeym suffered a 7 BTC private-key compromise. He reported it in China and engaged SlowMist. Those stolen coins moved toward Wasabi. That is a different story from the Gate freeze.

Gate locked the whole account. It held about $3 million then and roughly $1.5 million after the later market slide, per both ZachXBT and xxxkeym. The Guntur order hands that seized pool to the complainant as interim custody.

Why the Mislabel Matters

Why did it matter? A pig-butchering probe can still seize the wrong Gate balance when bridge rails get tagged as scam proceeds. Patterns like the Chen Zhi scam empire show why romance-investment tracing stays hard. A court can still convert “linked” exchange UIDs into USDT for the first victim on the complaint.

New rails change the surface of tracing. The human failure mode stays old. Treat a compliance tag as a verdict. Skip the dormant cold-wallet provenance. Let a press release outrun the mempool. CID’s public story remains a busted Rs 15 crore racket with eight arrests. ZachXBT’s ledger story is that Merlin bridge BTC, not alibarbit.bit loot, sat under xxxkeym’s Gate freeze. The user has been locked out for nearly sixteen months while the order to pay the complainant advances.

Unknowns remain. Gate has not published a technical rebuttal of the Merlin labeling claim. CID has not released a full public hop-by-hop chart tying the Tenali victim’s coins into those four UIDs beyond the press summary. The court file is an interim custody order, not a finished restitution trial with opposing expert evidence on the record. What the wire does put down is sharp enough. In ZachXBT’s telling, Indian CID’s Gate Merlin bridge freeze rests on mistaking bridge rails for scam proceeds. A Guntur court has told Gate to convert the seized accounts for the complainant anyway.

fullContent:
EDINBURGH, SCOTLAND—In response to the packed November video game release slate, Rockstar Games announced in a press statement Tuesday that it was delaying Grand Theft Auto VI to avoid competition with the release of Horny Mahjong: The Witches Of Panty Mountain. “We worked so hard on GTA VI, we’d hate to see it become just a small footnote in the zeitgeist as the new Horny Mahjong game inevitably dominates the gaming news cycle,” said Strauss Zelnick, CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive, adding that the company learned from its mistake after abysmal sales of Red Dead Redemption 2 were attributed to its release on the same day as Horny Mahjong: Soaking Wet Waifus Of Atlantis. “We hope players will be ready for a new game in late 2028, by which point they will have had ample time to finish the new Horny Mahjong and unlock all the secret pin-up cards. Then GTA VI will be able to have its time in the spotlight.” At press time, Zelnick was reportedly considering canceling GTA VI entirely after the announcement that a remastered 10th-anniversary edition of Horny Mahjong: Busty Maid Academy was scheduled for a November 2028 release.

title: Xsolla ZK Introduces a Gas Token Designed to Let Digital Items Move Between Games and Players
description:
Los Angeles, United States, 17th November 2026, Chainwire
The post Xsolla ZK Introduces a Gas Token Designed to Let Digital Items Move Between Games and Players appeared first on The Daily Hodl.
fullContent:
November 17th, 2026 – Los Angeles, United States

class=”ql-align-justify”>Xsolla ZK, Inc. is introducing Xsolla Gas (XLA), the native token of Xsolla ZK, a blockchain network for games.

XLA is designed to pay the network fees that arise when players transfer or share eligible digital items on Xsolla ZK. Players who prefer not to download and set up a separate wallet can cover those fees through Xsolla Gas Station, offered by Xsolla (USA), Inc., a global commerce company, where they buy XLA-NT, a non-transferable gas credit used only to pay network fees on Xsolla ZK. Xsolla Gas Station sells only XLA-NT. Xsolla Gas pays the network fees that let players transfer the eligible in-game digital items they own.

Players want more from the games and brands they follow, and developers want ways to engage players. Digital items have become more than cosmetics; players can now collect them from their favorite games. But letting players keep, share, and give away those items can be complicated.

Most digital items today live on a single game’s backend. Players generally can’t transfer them to friends or use them in another game, and items become inaccessible if a game shuts down. Blockchain-backed items stay with the players who collect them, but transferring them requires a network fee. Players typically have to set up and manage a separate digital wallet and get the right token to pay that fee, which adds complexity.

Xsolla ZK is designed to lower these barriers. Xsolla’s existing payment, monetization, and distribution products can now use blockchain-backed items, giving developers a new way to monetize and distribute digital items and giving players new ways to keep them and give them to other players. Players use Xsolla Gas to cover the network fees required to transfer or share a digital item held in their Xsolla Backpack.

Xsolla Backpack is an inventory for the digital items a player owns. Digital items issued to the Backpack in transferable form are designed to remain available to the player even if the issuing game shuts down. A player can give them to another player. This blockchain functionality is designed to empower players to decide what happens to the eligible items they own. Digital items that remain on a game’s own backend continue to work as they do today and cannot be transferred through Backpack.

Players who want to collect these digital items sign in to their account as usual, without needing a seed phrase or a separate wallet setup. They cover network fees by buying XLA-NT gas credits through Xsolla Gas Station, using the payment methods they already know and prefer. Players can collect eligible items they purchase or claim in their Backpack and share them with other players.

“Players should be able to share and gift digital items they own, anytime, anywhere, with anyone they know,” said Chris Hewish, President of Xsolla (USA). “Developers gain a new way to monetize their games, and players gain eligible digital items that are theirs to keep. When both sides win, the games do too. We are adding options inside the tools they already use, not asking anyone to change how they work.”

When a player wants to share or give away a digital item, the transaction runs on Xsolla ZK, the blockchain network, and the network fee is paid in Xsolla Gas. This lets players hold items and give them to other players, and it is designed to let them carry items between supported games. Players can pay the fee themselves in XLA or XLA-NT. Developers and partners can also use XLA to pay network fees for their item activity.

Players can cover network fees through:

  • Xsolla Gas Station: players sign in with their Xsolla ID and buy XLA-NT gas credits through the checkout they already use. Xsolla Gas Station sells only XLA-NT, which can be used only to pay network fees.
  • Crypto exchanges: XLA is available on crypto exchanges, including Kraken, LBank, and Biconomy, in supported markets.

More than 1,500 game teams use Xsolla (USA)’s tools and services to monetize and distribute games. These tools are designed to work with Xsolla ZK to support the transfer of eligible digital items, and Xsolla Backpack and Xsolla Gas Station are now available without additional development for teams using compatible Xsolla (USA) products, integrating with existing player and payment flows. Studios, publishers, brands, and players can learn more about Xsolla Gas Station at x.la/gas.

Developers building games, wallets, marketplaces, and item services on Xsolla ZK can find network documentation, developer tools, and integration paths at xsolla.org.

Readers can also complete a short Xsolla Quest at xsolla.pro/xsolla-zk-quest to learn more about Xsolla Gas, Xsolla Gas Station, and Xsolla Backpack.

What is Xsolla Quest? Xsolla Quest lets people complete a few simple steps on an Xsolla page to receive an item.

About Xsolla

Xsolla (USA) is a global commerce company that builds and provides all the things developers need to launch, grow, and monetize video games. Headquartered in Los Angeles, California, the company supports studios of every size, from indie to AAA, with solutions across direct-to-consumer commerce, intelligent payments, entertainment-based IP, and player engagement products. Xsolla (USA) helps developers fund, distribute, market, and monetize their games at scale. Trusted by more than 70% of the top 100 highest-grossing games, Xsolla (USA) operates as the merchant of record across 200+ geographies with access to 1,000+ local payment methods worldwide. Grounded in a deep belief in the future of video games, Xsolla (USA) is resolute in bringing opportunities together and unlocking growth for creators everywhere.

For more information, visit xsolla.com.

About Xsolla ZK

Xsolla ZK is an Ethereum Layer 2 network for games, built as a ZK rollup. Its gas token, XLA, is an ERC-20 token on Ethereum mainnet with a total supply of 1 billion. XLA becomes the base token of Xsolla ZK through the canonical bridge. Every transaction on the network, including claiming a game item, pays gas in XLA. Users can pay in XLA-NT, a non-transferable gas credit used only to pay network fees on Xsolla ZK.

For more information on Xsolla ZK, visit xsolla.org

Xsolla Gas Station and XLA-NT are offered by Xsolla (USA), Inc. Xsolla Gas Station sells only XLA-NT. XLA-NT is a non-transferable credit that can be used only to pay network fees on Xsolla ZK. It cannot be transferred or sold and cannot be redeemed for cash or other crypto. XLA and XLA-NT are designed for paying network fees and are not offered as investments. Crypto prices can change quickly. Xsolla (USA)’s Web3 products are not offered to, and may not be used by, any person or entity that is: (a) located or resident in any country, territory, or U.S. state where Xsolla (USA) restricts access; (b) subject to applicable sanctions, or owned or controlled by a sanctioned party; or (c) otherwise barred by local law from using them.

title: Revolut Wants to Put Private Equity on the Blockchain
description:
Key Takeaways Gilbert promised four blockchain-enabled private-market funds. Revolut already sells private-fund stakes from €1. Current terms ban selling to […]
The post Revolut Wants to Put Private Equity on the Blockchain appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Gilbert promised four blockchain-enabled private-market funds.
  • Revolut already sells private-fund stakes from €1.
  • Current terms ban selling to other investors.
  • Tokenized private funds rarely trade after issuance.

Revolut chair Martin Gilbert outlined the four funds at Solana’s Breakpoint conference in London on November 17, Cointelegraph reported.

Gilbert told the audience that customers buying a private equity fund on Revolut, once the new products launch, would be able to do so in fractional amounts. Blockchain, he said, would split funds holding illiquid assets “into what I would term marketable sizes.” He tied the plan to a warning that finance may be heading into a liquidity crunch, sharpest in private markets, and argued that those markets need more buyers – something he said only a blockchain-enabled structure could attract.

Revolut has not named the funds’ strategies, managers, minimum investments or launch date. Nor has it said which blockchain they would run on; the Solana stage does not settle that question.

The Crunch Behind the Pitch

Gilbert’s warning has a recent reference point. In June, Partners Group capped withdrawals from its $8.6 billion Global Value SICAV after investors asked to pull 9.8% of the fund’s assets in a single quarter, against a limit of 5%, Bloomberg reported. Private credit funds at Apollo, BlackRock, Blue Owl and Morgan Stanley had restricted withdrawals during the same period.

Partners Group and Apollo are two of the four managers whose funds Revolut already distributes, although the capped Global Value SICAV is not the Partners Group fund offered in the Revolut app. The episode shows what “semi-liquid” means in practice: when too many holders head for the exit at once, the fund decides how many get out.

What €1 Already Buys on Revolut

Fractional access is not new at Revolut. Since its July 27 launch, eligible customers in several European countries have been able to put as little as €1 into private equity, private credit and infrastructure funds from Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane and Partners Group. The products are ELTIFs – European Long-Term Investment Funds, an EU fund format that the ELTIF 2.0 overhaul opened to retail investors in 2024 by removing the old €10,000 minimum. Revolut sells them as evergreen funds, with no end date and periodic windows for redemption requests.

Getting out is the constraint. Revolut’s investment terms for Spanish residents bar customers from transferring private fund holdings to another broker or platform and from selling them on a secondary market. The holdings sit in an omnibus account – a pooled position Revolut holds on behalf of all its customers – so an individual investor has no separately registered stake to take elsewhere. Revolut also warns that redemptions are not guaranteed and can be capped or suspended, and its suitability guidance describes a commitment measured in years.

Under these rules, the fund’s own redemption window is the only way out. That is the rule Gilbert’s funds would need to change. Slicing a fund into smaller pieces leaves it untouched.

READ MORE:

Solana at $1,100? – What Bitwise’s Bull Case Needs

Tokenized Funds Exist – Their Holders Rarely Trade

Two of Revolut’s managers have already put private funds on blockchains. Apollo and Securitize launched ACRED, a tokenized feeder into Apollo’s Diversified Credit Fund, in January 2025, issuing it on Aptos, Avalanche, Ethereum, Ink, Polygon and Solana for accredited investors. Hamilton Lane has offered tokenized feeder funds through Securitize on Polygon since 2023, and in August 2024 it opened its Secondary Fund VI to qualified investors with a $20,000 minimum, down from the usual $5 million.

Those products cut the entry ticket. Whether holders then trade with each other is a separate question, and the evidence so far points one way. A Macquarie University study of tokenized real-world assets found that most tokens see low trading volumes, long holding periods and few active participants, and it named whitelisting rules and regulatory gating among the barriers. Investors in these products behave much as they would in the traditional versions: they subscribe, hold and redeem through the issuer.

Pricing creates a second problem. A private fund’s net asset value is an appraisal published monthly or quarterly. A token sold to another investor fetches whatever that investor will pay, and in a year when holders across private funds have been trying to leave together, that price can sit well below the last valuation. A blockchain records who owns the token and moves it cleanly between accounts; it does not supply the buyer.

Four Questions for Revolut’s Fund Documents

Who can hold the tokens?

Only verified Revolut accounts, or outside wallets as well?

Where can they change hands?

Inside the app, on a regulated trading venue, or directly onchain?

Who sets the price?

The last published valuation, or buyers and sellers in real time?

What happens in a rush?

Do redemption caps still bind when secondary buyers disappear?

Fees and any lock-up period will also decide whether a small stake is worth holding. Success would be easy to recognise: a Revolut customer selling part of a private fund to another investor, outside a redemption window, at a price both sides can see.

fullContent:
Bitcoin (BTC USD) closed last week at $65,351, its first weekly close below the 200-week moving average since August. On Monday, November 16, market maker Wintermute warned that it expects “pressure into the $50s.” The 200-week average, Bitcoin’s average weekly close over roughly four years, sits near $68,000.

River, a Bitcoin broker, pointed out the other side of the story. Bitcoin has traded below that line only about 8% of its life, and buying there has paid off in the past.

We checked every week since 2014. BTC USD has dipped under the average ten times before. Seven of those dips lasted two weeks or less, and only the 2022 bear market went as deep as Wintermute’s target.

So who is right about BTC USD: the trader’s warning or the history?

Bitcoin has only been below its 200-week moving average for 8.4% of its lifetime.

Average return on bitcoin bought during these periods:

1 year later: +120%
3 years later: +582% pic.twitter.com/ob1U57jmhj

— River (@River) November 16, 2026

Wintermute’s Bitcoin Warning: “The ETF Bid Is Gone”

In its November 16 market update, Wintermute said: “We haven’t cleared the bear market yet.” It called the rally off the July low “a fake-out.” Bitcoin fell 12.7% last week while the S&P 500 gained 2.5%.

Its case rests on money flows:

  • ETFs: U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are about $1.9 billion net negative for 2026, after $21 billion of inflows in 2025.
  • Stablecoins: supply is down $14 billion to $16 billion in 30 days, so “no fresh dollars are arriving.” DefiLlama’s data agrees, showing a $16.1 billion drop to $288.2 billion.
  • Rates: markets price a December Fed rate hike at about 92%, and the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.15%. Bitcoin pays no yield, so it gets sold first.
  • Liquidations: about $1.7 billion was liquidated in the 24 hours into Sunday, 80% of it long bets. Wintermute reads the bounce since then as short covering, not new buying.

Wintermute names Saturday’s $62,000 low as the first level and the $60,000 options cluster on Deribit as “the next magnet.” It would turn less defensive only if BTC USD closes a day back above the 200-week average near $68,000. Net ETF inflows that same day are its second condition.

Even Wintermute adds a caveat: closes below the 200-week average “remain interesting for patient, high-conviction capital on a multi-quarter view.”

DISCOVER: Top 20 Crypto to Buy in 2026

BTC USD Below the 200-Week Average: Every Past Case Since 2014

River’s post says Bitcoin has spent 8.4% of its life below the 200-week average, with average returns of 120% a year later and 582% three years later. Our own count of weekly closes since the average first existed in 2014 gives 8.3%.

  • Most dips were short: seven of the ten earlier stretches lasted one or two weeks, and none of those went more than 5% below the average.
  • 2022 was the exception: two stretches that year, the second lasting 30 weeks and reaching 32% below the average after the FTX collapse.
  • One year later: in all eight cases with a full year of data, BTC USD was higher than at its first weekly close below the line. The gains ranged from 22% after 2022 to 1,000% after the March 2020 crash.
  • This year: BTC dipped under the line for a week in late June and again in August, and recovered both times.

Wintermute’s target is what makes this week different. A move into the $50,000s means trading 12% to 27% below the average. In 12 years, only 2022 went that deep.

DISCOVER: BTC USD Hits $62,006 After a Weekend Dump: Did MARA’s Bitcoin Sales Cause It?

BTC USD Price Analysis: The 200-Week Line Is Now Resistance

On the weekly chart, where each candle covers one week, BTC USD trades at $64,419. It sits below its 200-week simple moving average (SMA), a plain average of the past 200 weekly closes, at $68,191, and its 50-week SMA at $74,516.

  • Resistance: $68,191, the 200-week average. Above it, $75,000, a level that has turned Bitcoin several times since March 2024, most recently in September.
  • Support: $61,000, where the 2021 high meets this year’s February and November lows. Below it, $53,000, where the 2021 highs and 2024 lows meet, inside Wintermute’s target zone.

BTCUSDT 1W chart. Source: TradingView

Path What has to happen Next stop
Push higher A weekly close back above the 200-week average, $68,191, with ETF inflows $75,000 and the 50-week average
Stall Weekly closes between $61,000 and $68,191 A base like the brief dips of 2023
Slip A weekly close below $61,000 $53,000, inside Wintermute’s $50,000s

DISCOVER: The 12+ Hottest Crypto Presales to Buy Right Now

History favors BTC USD buyers below the 200-week average, but only if this dip behaves like the short ones. The flows Wintermute points to look more like 2022. A weekly close back above $68,191 would settle the argument in favor of the history. Until then, the trader’s warning stands.

Yet SOL holders aren’t exactly celebrating as the token remains deep in correction territory after falling from its September highs at $125. With Wall Street knocking on Solana’s door, holders now face a tempting question: Is a $90 recovery finally coming, or does SOL have another painful trip toward $60?

Solana (SOL)

NYSE Owner ICE Eyes Solana Validator as Network Ditches Beta Label

ICE is considering operating a Solana validator, according to comments from ICE Clear Europe President Hester Serafini at Solana Breakpoint in London yesterday. Validators help secure Solana’s network and participate in transaction processing and consensus. Having one of the world’s largest financial market operators participate could strengthen Solana’s institutional credibility.

ICE is already preparing for a closer relationship with the blockchain. Its planned tokenized securities trading infrastructure can accept tokens minted on Solana. The company hasn’t confirmed a validator launch, but the possibility puts Solana firmly on Wall Street’s radar.

The announcement also follows the Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation’s November 12 plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana during the second half of 2027. The DTCC sits at the heart of US securities settlement, making the development another important institutional milestone.

Solana is also making a major change under the hood. Also last night, the Solana Foundation announced that the network had officially dropped its Mainnet Beta designation, introducing Solana 1.0.

The transition marks years of Solana’s development as the network moves toward a more mature production environment. Its Alpenglow upgrade targets 150-millisecond transaction finality, while Firedancer introduces another independently developed validator client.

In other words, Solana isn’t just chasing faster transactions anymore. It’s positioning itself as infrastructure for financial markets that cannot afford to move at internet meme speed.

fullContent:
Four states have banned cryptocurrency kiosks this year as scams tied to the machines cost Americans nearly $389 million in 2025.

The FBI says it received 13,460 complaints involving crypto kiosks in 2025.

Reported losses jumped 58% from the year before.

People older than 50 filed more than half of the complaints and reported over $302,000,000 in losses.

Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont have enacted statewide bans, reports Stateline.

Hawaii also barred consumers from depositing cash into kiosks to buy crypto under a law that took effect in October.

At least 20 Massachusetts communities have banned the machines as of August.

Jackson, Michigan and Star, Idaho, have passed bans of their own.

Attorneys general in Iowa, Massachusetts and the District of Columbia have sued kiosk operators.

They allege the operators failed to put adequate safeguards against fraud in place.

An Iowa attorney general investigation found that 98% of transactions at Bitcoin Depot kiosks in the state were linked to scams.

The figure was 94% at CoinFlip kiosks.

Bitcoin Depot has since filed for bankruptcy. It cited restrictive state regulations and bans. The company took its kiosks offline in May.

Operators have pushed back.

They argue the machines serve legitimate customers and that stronger fraud safeguards would better protect consumers than prohibitions.

Says Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director,

“Every day that these laws aren’t passed are days where victims are having money stolen from them, and that money, because it’s through cryptocurrency and the nature of the kiosk, it’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back.”

title: Solana at $1,100? – What Bitwise’s Bull Case Needs
description:
Key Takeaways Bull case needs 46x today’s network revenue Bitwise values that scenario near $442 today Fee model relies on […]
The post Solana at $1,100? – What Bitwise’s Bull Case Needs appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Bull case needs 46x today’s network revenue
  • Bitwise values that scenario near $442 today
  • Fee model relies on open, bot-heavy trading
  • Regulated tokenized stocks arrive behind permission walls

Bitwise’s November 16 research, written by Kam Benbrik and Rafal Klich, builds a five-year SOL valuation on tokenized stock trading and sets its base case at $385.

The arithmetic behind $1,100

The white paper’s model starts with Real Economic Value, or REV: the fees users pay to use Solana, including priority fees and tips. Bitwise multiplies projected 2031 REV by a valuation multiple, divides by an assumed supply of 700 million SOL, then discounts the result back to today.

Bitwise’s 2031 scenarios
Input Bear Base Bull
Annual REV $2.80B $6.75B $12.83B
REV multiple 20x 40x 60x
2031 outlook $80 $385 $1,100
Present value $32 $155 $442

In the bull case, that works out to a network valued near $770 billion. Two choices inside the model pull against the headline figure. The 700 million supply assumption sits above today’s roughly 635 million SOL, so issuance between now and 2031 dilutes each token. And the 20% annual discount rate, which Bitwise attributes to risks around tokenization pace, regulation and execution, is about double the 8–10% typical for large-cap equities.

Discounting changes how the bull case reads today. The paper’s third-quarter calculations use a SOL price of around $100. Measured against that, Bitwise’s own present value for the $1,100 scenario is roughly four times the reference price, not eleven.

Revenue has to do the work, not the multiple

Solana’s annualized network revenue in the third quarter of 2026 was $278 million, according to the paper. On that run rate, Bitwise estimates SOL trades at roughly 230 times revenue.

Every scenario therefore assumes the multiple shrinks, to 60x even in the bull case. The upside has to come from revenue. By Coindoo’s calculation, bull-case REV is about 46 times the third-quarter run rate, the base case about 24 times and the bear case about 10 times.

The network’s revenue is also a shrinking slice of what Solana activity generates. Bitwise’s data shows applications keeping a rising share of combined revenue since early 2025, so more trading does not lift network fees one-for-one.

Three trading inputs produce those revenue figures:

Tokenized share of global stock and ETF volume

3% / 4% / 5%

Solana’s share of tokenized stock trading

30% / 50% / 65%

Turnover versus traditional stocks

2x / 2.5x / 3x

Bear / base / bull values from Bitwise’s white paper.

The first input is measured against roughly $235 trillion in annual global stock and ETF trading. Because the three inputs multiply, small changes compound. Moving all three from base to bull nearly doubles the trading Solana would handle, which is why bull-case REV is close to twice the base case.

Where the fee estimate comes from

To convert trading into fees, Bitwise sampled instructions involving tokenized assets on Solana during the third quarter of 2026. For each successful swap, it counted about three failed transactions and two supporting ones.

The failed transactions are mostly arbitrage attempts that lost the auction for transaction ordering. That is normal in competitive onchain markets, where several bots chase the same price gap and only one wins. Supporting transactions cover transfers, orders, liquidity provision and price feeds.

Fees around one successful swap
Type Count Avg fee Fee share*
Successful swap 1 $0.052 ~66%
Failed attempt ~3 $0.007 ~27%
Supporting ~2 $0.003 ~8%

*Coindoo calculation from Bitwise’s counts and average fees; blended fee about $0.0133 per transaction.

About a third of the modeled fees therefore come from activity around a trade rather than the trade itself. That ratio was measured on venues where anyone can run an arbitrage bot. Applying it to 2031 assumes tokenized stock trading keeps the same competitive structure.

The regulated version looks different

The compliant tokenized-equity markets taking shape now restrict who can trade, and that cuts against the conditions behind the fee sample.

The SEC’s Innovation Exemption for tokenized NMS stock limits trading to permissioned participants and lets each venue set its own access standards. It also caps the number of symbols and the trading volume, though the fact sheet gives no figures. Holders must receive the same entitlements as owners of the traditional shares, products that only offer synthetic exposure are excluded, and the relief runs for five years.

Galaxy’s tokenized GLXY shares already live on Solana as SEC-registered Class A common stock, with Superstate as digital transfer agent. Holders can self-custody them, but transfers run bilaterally between allowlisted entities, and Galaxy has not enabled AMM-based trading.

Nasdaq’s product comes later. Its September 10 announcement expects Nasdaq Equity Tokens to launch with Payward, Kraken’s parent company, in the second quarter of 2027, alongside a $100 million Nasdaq Ventures investment in Payward. The release names no blockchain. Bitwise’s plan to record its Solana ETF’s ownership onchain also keeps transfer limits in place.

Fewer participants means fewer bots competing for each trade. If permissioned venues settle on Solana but produce fewer failed and supporting transactions per swap, the same trading volume would yield less REV than Bitwise’s sample implies. The exemption’s volume cap could also slow progress toward the tokenization share in the model for as long as it applies.

Why the multiple carries so much weight

REV is gross network fees, not profit. Under Solana’s fee rules, half of each base fee is burned and half goes to the validator, while priority fees go entirely to validators. Burning shrinks supply for every holder. Validator income pays the operators running the network, and stakers can receive part of it depending on how their validator shares rewards. Unstaked SOL receives none of it directly.

The multiple is Bitwise’s judgment of what those fees are worth to a token holder. Holding bull-case revenue and supply fixed, it moves the result as much as any trading input:

Coindoo sensitivity: $12.83B REV, 700M SOL
Multiple Implied SOL value
20x About $367
40x About $733
60x About $1,100

At the base-case 40x multiple, reaching $1,100 would take about $19.25 billion in annual REV, roughly 69 times the third-quarter run rate.

The figures that would test the scenario

Each input behind Bitwise’s top scenario can be checked onchain or in public filings, which makes the model testable from one quarter to the next.

  1. Quarterly REV against the $278 million Q3 2026 baseline
  2. The share of REV coming from tokenized assets
  3. Failed and supporting transactions per tokenized swap
  4. Whether GLXY or other registered shares gain secondary trading

title: Akash Unveils GPU Forward Contracts Ahead of 2027 Pilot
description:
Akash unveiled Akash GPU forward contracts, branded Akash Forwards, on November 17, 2026, at Solana Breakpoint. Founder Greg Osuri outlined a cleared forward market for future GPU capacity. The contracts are built for physical delivery of verified compute. They are not a cash bet on a synthetic index. The BusinessWire release sets a Q1 2027 […]
The post Akash Unveils GPU Forward Contracts Ahead of 2027 Pilot appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
Akash unveiled Akash GPU forward contracts, branded Akash Forwards, on November 17, 2026, at Solana Breakpoint. Founder Greg Osuri outlined a cleared forward market for future GPU capacity. The contracts are built for physical delivery of verified compute. They are not a cash bet on a synthetic index. The BusinessWire release sets a Q1 2027 pilot for certified participants. A wider public launch is targeted for Q2 2027.

The product page is blunt about the present tense. Akash Compute Forwards is a published market design. It is not open, and nothing on that site trades yet.

What Akash GPU Forward Contracts Are Trying to Buy

Most AI labs still lock GPUs the hard way. They sign private, bilateral deals. Hardware grades, regions, lengths, and prices rarely match across contracts. When supply tightens, weaker buyers get outbid. When plans change, they sit on capacity they no longer need. Investors and lenders face the same fog. Without a public forward price tied to deliverable machines, valuing the AI buildout stays guesswork.

Akash Forwards treats one unit as a node-month. In the design, a buyer can lock eight-GPU NVIDIA B300 nodes for calendar months ahead. Other grades include H200s and RTX Pro 6000 Blackwells. The price is fixed when the trade clears. Each contract names a GPU grade, a region, and a delivery month. Both sides then trade against a common standard.

Eligible providers whose hardware passes Akash verification can sell future capacity before it comes online. Buyers can sell contracts back into the market before delivery if their plans change. Prices form in a daily open call auction. An automated clearing program sits between every buyer and seller. It manages daily settlement in U.S. dollars.

How Delivery Is Supposed to Work

Follow one filled position through the published timeline. The contract trades at daily calls until shortly before its month. Price changes settle in dollars every day. Right after the last call for that month, the program pairs each remaining buyer with attested nodes. It then records a one-month lease.

Every hour of the month is checked. Akash validators inspect each lease on an hourly cadence. Providers are paid for hours they serve. If a provider stops serving, the buyer does not pay for the miss. The system then looks for replacement compute through the spot path. On a longer outage, the design offers two exits. A buyer may finish the month on one node. Or the buyer may take the rest of the month in cash at a reference price.

That is the physical-delivery claim in one line. You get attested GPU hours for the month you bought. Or you get a cash gap when delivery fails. The chain job, as described, is lease accounting and hourly checks. It is not a proof that a model trained on those GPUs was correct.

Why This Matters for AI Compute Pricing

Cheng Wang is chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Overclock Labs, the creator of Akash Network. In the release, he said three U.S. exchanges have already announced compute futures in 2026. He argued that settlement trust is still the open question for those contracts. He also said bilateral GPU deals hide the prices buyers and sellers need. In the project's framing, Akash Forwards answers that problem the way power and gas markets did. Every contract delivers real GPU-hours to a defined standard. Every recorded price is one somebody paid.

Greg Osuri put the buyer pain more simply. Unless a lab is among the best funded, he said, it cannot see what compute really costs. It gets outbid when capacity is tight. It overbuys to stay safe. That uncertainty climbs to investors trying to value the AI buildout. A public forward curve for standardized node-months is the core bet. AI and blockchain rails would turn opaque capacity into a commodity-style price signal. That sits next to other experiments that turn capital into a claim on compute. One parallel is 0G's path from staked assets into AI compute credits.

What Is Demonstrated, and Where the Catch Sits

What the primary record shows today is an unveil, not a live book. Osuri announced Akash Forwards at Breakpoint. The company published a white paper and design site at forwards.akash.network. The wire names the hardware grades and the month-long physical unit. It also names the daily auction, dollar clearing, the Q1 2027 certified pilot, and the Q2 2027 public target. Simulated terminal prices on the design site are marked as illustrative.

What remains project claim is harder. The pilot has not cleared a real trade. Default protection, certification agents, guarantors, and assignment rules are design layers. They are not yet a proven market with depth. Hourly validator checks can attest that a lease ran. They do not prove that replacement capacity will always be available at a fair price. Wang's comparison to power markets is an analogy for how forward prices can finance supply. It is not evidence that GPU forwards will attract the same liquidity.

The mental model to keep is simple. Akash GPU forward contracts try to put a public, physical-delivery price on future AI capacity. That price would come before anyone has to guess from private deals. Watch whether the Q1 2027 pilot clears real node-months at verified grades. Watch whether those prices stay visible after assignment. Watch whether buyers treat the curve as a hedge rather than a brochure.

The post Akash Unveils GPU Forward Contracts Ahead of 2027 Pilot appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
