title: Bitcoin Falls to Four-Month Low Near $62,000 as CZ Denies Binance Sold Crypto
description:
Bitcoin slid to a four-month low of $62,006 on November 15, triggering a wave of liquidations and fresh rumors that Binance was dumping its holdings. Binance co-founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao
The post Bitcoin Falls to Four-Month Low Near $62,000 as CZ Denies Binance Sold Crypto appeared first on NFT Plazas.
fullContent:
Bitcoin slid to a four-month low of $62,006 on November 15, triggering a wave of liquidations and fresh rumors that Binance was dumping its holdings. Binance co-founder Changpeng “CZ” Zhao moved quickly to shut that narrative down.

“No, Binance did not sell crypto,” Zhao wrote on X. By 5:15 a.m. UTC on November 16, Bitcoin had recovered to $64,615, according to CoinGecko, though it remained down roughly 13.5% over seven days.

The episode raises a pointed question for traders: can a single denial calm fears of an exchange-driven sell-off when the forces weighing on the market run far deeper?

CZ: “Correlation Does Not Prove Causation”

Zhao’s post did more than deny. He said he had been buying, not selling: “I bought crypto in the past few days, as I got some stablecoins recently.” He then joked, “maybe this is the cause.“

He listed several possible drivers of the slide: institutional withdrawals from spot ETFs, expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening, lingering security fears, and retail investors raising cash for Anthropic’s IPO. He stopped short of blaming any single factor. “No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation,” he wrote.

Binance is privately held, so there is no public stock or filing to settle the question. For now, markets have only CZ’s word.

CZ Denies Binance Sold Crypto (Source: X)

ETF Outflows and a Leverage Flush

The clearest pressure has come from Wall Street. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs logged about $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven straight trading sessions through November 13, according to SoSoValue. The final day alone saw roughly $185.5 million leave, led by BlackRock’s IBIT at $143.5 million and Fidelity’s FBTC at $41.9 million.

Leverage amplified the drop. CoinGlass data showed about $241 million in positions liquidated in the 24 hours through November 16, including $105.8 million in Bitcoin. Some market-wide tallies covering the full weekend slide put total liquidations closer to $2 billion.

When prices fall, exchanges automatically close leveraged positions that can no longer meet margin requirements, forcing more selling. That cascade explains the speed of both the plunge and the bounce. Crowded long positions were flushed out, rather than replaced by a fresh wave of sellers.

Bitcoin ETF Flow (Source: Fairside Investors)

A Liquidation Event, Not Yet a Reversal

For traders, the weekend looked liquidation-driven rather than a clear trend change. Three signals will show whether the rebound is real: a recovery of key moving averages on rising volume, funding rates moving from negative back to neutral, and $62,000 holding on any retest.

A bounce on fading volume would raise the odds of another test lower. The first rally after a liquidation flush is rarely one to chase blindly.

The Shadow of the Binance Hack

The rumors found fertile ground because of the October 29 Binance breach, in which attackers stole more than $6 billion in digital assets across multiple blockchains. The FBI attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group. Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said about $2.8 billion of the stolen funds had been frozen by November 3.

Institutional investors have trimmed Bitcoin ETF exposure since the hack. With confidence already shaken, any large movement linked to an exchange is quickly read as a warning sign. That is why CZ’s denial drew so much attention.

Anthropic IPO and Macro Headwinds

CZ’s most unusual suggestion was that capital may be rotating toward Anthropic’s upcoming Nasdaq listing, expected under the ticker ANT. The Crypto Times reported that Binance’s ANTHROPICUSDT pre-IPO perpetual contract implied a valuation of about $1.39 trillion on November 10. That was down 35% from a September peak of $2.13 trillion. Such contracts offer price exposure, not ownership.

CZ also highlighted a comparison from macro analyst Matt Cole. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX’s June IPO, then gained 28% over the following 100 days. Bitcoin has dropped about 18% over a similar window ahead of Anthropic’s debut, though past patterns guarantee nothing.

Macro conditions add weight. Unexpectedly firm U.S. inflation has revived expectations of another Fed rate hike. Higher rates and a stronger dollar typically cool demand for risk assets such as Bitcoin.

Key Levels: $62,000 Is the Line

Bitcoin broke below its 200-week moving average near $68,000 during the slide, a level many traders treat as a long-term floor. Support now sits at $62,000. A sustained break below it would bring the $60,000 zone into focus.

On the upside, resistance stands near $65,600, followed by the $68,000 to $70,000 band. A close above that range could spark a short-term bullish trend.

What Comes Next

CZ’s denial may ease fears that Binance itself was dumping assets, but debunking a rumor does not create buying pressure. Until fresh capital returns, the short-term outlook leans neutral to bearish, with bulls and bears increasingly divided after the flush.

Zhao remains upbeat on the bigger picture. “Mid-long term, crypto will continue to grow,” he wrote, noting that his views were personal and not financial advice.

For now, ETF flow data, Federal Reserve signals and Anthropic’s listing are likely to set Bitcoin’s next move. Related assets to watch include BTC and Binance’s BNB token.

title: Ethereum Price and $1.16B Selling Threat: North Korea’s Binance Hacker Moves $137M
description:
Ethereum price battles pressure as North Korea's Binance hacker moves $137M in ETH, leaving another $1.16B potentially awaiting liquidation.
The post Ethereum Price and $1.16B Selling Threat: North Korea’s Binance Hacker Moves $137M appeared first on Cryptonews.
fullContent:
Ethereum price is facing another challenge as a North Korea-linked hacker moves $137 million in ETH. The massive transfer comes as ETH USD struggles to defend $1,800 after falling from a $1,840 high yesterday.

Wallets linked to the October Binance hack still reportedly hold $1.16 billion in Ethereum. Another $1.19 billion sits in Bitcoin, leaving the attacker with a staggering crypto reserve. With 74,881 ETH suddenly dispersed across multiple addresses, we have another reason to watch the Ethereum price.

Ethereum (ETH)
24h7d30d1yAll time

A $2.35 Billion Shadow Hangs Over Ethereum

The latest transaction is part of a much larger operation that has kept blockchain investigators watching the stolen funds. According to Arkham data, the attacker dispersed 74,881 ETH worth $137 million within an hour.

The movement followed the disposal of most of the attacker’s stolen altcoins. The remaining stash is now heavily concentrated in Bitcoin and Ethereum, with 632,000 ETH and 18,362 BTC still sitting in associated wallets.

That leaves $2.35 billion in crypto potentially moving through the laundering pipeline. The timing could hardly be worse for Ethereum as its price has already suffered a sharp correction, with the latest sell-off pushing ETH below $1,800 after trading near $1,850.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

North Korea’s Binance Hacker Still Holds $1.16 Billion in ETH

The October 29 Binance attack was one of the largest crypto thefts ever recorded. The FBI attributed the operation to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, identifying more than $6 billion in stolen virtual assets.

Investigators said the attackers converted stolen assets primarily into Ether. They also warned that the funds could move through decentralized finance protocols and instant swap services during subsequent laundering stages.

Now, the latest 74,881 ETH transfer shows the operation is entering another significant phase.

The hacker’s remaining crypto stash:

  • Ethereum: 632,000 ETH, worth $1.16 billion.
  • Bitcoin: 18,362 BTC, worth $1.19 billion.
  • Recently dispersed: 74,881 ETH, worth $137 million.

The sheer size of the remaining Ethereum position is particularly concerning. If the attacker continues fragmenting these holdings, thousands of smaller transactions could make tracking and intervention increasingly difficult. Cross-chain swaps could also move funds beyond Ethereum’s immediate ecosystem.

The market now has another potential source of selling pressure to monitor. Even a fraction of the remaining stash entering liquid markets could become a significant event.

Ethereum Price Faces Another Test Below $1,800

Ethereum’s technical picture was already looking uncomfortable before the latest hacker activity emerged. ETH recently plunged toward $1,712 before staging a partial recovery. The rebound struggled to regain momentum, leaving the Ethereum price below $1,800, down 14% over seven days.

Institutional demand has offered little immediate relief. U.S. spot Ether ETFs recorded $398.9 million in weekly outflows between November 9 and 13, adding another source of pressure.

Now, the North Korean hacker’s enormous Ethereum holdings introduce another uncomfortable variable. The $1,800 level has become an important psychological battleground. Losing it again could expose ETH to another round of panic selling, particularly if traders begin pricing in the possibility of additional stolen funds entering the market.

title: PYUSD Supply Drop Wipes $269M in a Day as Peg Holds
description:
PayPal USD (PYUSD) lost about $269 million of market value in 24 hours. That PYUSD supply drop of roughly 10% left the float near $2.38 billion. The price stayed at about $1. On CoinGecko’s stablecoin board, that was the sharpest one-day cut among the 30 largest dollar tokens at a late-night November 17 read. DefiLlama […]
The post PYUSD Supply Drop Wipes $269M in a Day as Peg Holds appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.
fullContent:
PayPal USD (PYUSD) lost about $269 million of market value in 24 hours. That PYUSD supply drop of roughly 10% left the float near $2.38 billion. The price stayed at about $1. On CoinGecko’s stablecoin board, that was the sharpest one-day cut among the 30 largest dollar tokens at a late-night November 17 read. DefiLlama printed a matching picture. Circulating PYUSD sat near $2.38 billion, down about $248 million, or roughly 9.5%, from the prior day.

That is the plain read. Tokens left circulation. The peg did not.

What the Boards Show

CoinGecko’s 24-hour print around 12:42 a.m. ET on November 17 put PYUSD near $2.38 billion after a $269.2 million, 10.2% cut. CoinMarketCap listed about 2.38 billion tokens in circulation at the same scale. Through the slide, the token traded between about $0.9994 and $1.00.

DefiLlama’s chain split sharpens where the float moved. Ethereum PYUSD fell from about $1.60 billion to about $1.46 billion in a day, a cut near 9%. Solana fell from about $803 million to about $694 million, a cut near 14%. Smaller rails such as Arbitrum barely moved. Public dashboards do not name which wallets redeemed, so the boards show size and chain, not the commercial reason.

The one-day hit sits inside a wider drawdown. CoinGecko’s daily series puts PYUSD near a $3.04 billion peak on October 27. From that high to the November 17 print, the float is down about $660 million, or roughly 22%. Over the latest seven days DefiLlama shows PYUSD circulating supply down about 14%. USDT and USDC each moved about 1% or less over the same week. In dollars, the giants still shed more absolute value. In percentage terms, PYUSD’s shrink is the outlier.

Paxos issues PYUSD for PayPal as a dollar stablecoin meant to redeem one-for-one into U.S. dollars for eligible holders. Neither PayPal nor Paxos had published a dedicated statement on this redemption window in the public materials checked here. The market boards are the primary receipt for the size of the cut.

What This PYUSD Supply Drop Is Actually Telling You

Here is the recurring question this print presses: when a payments-branded dollar token says it is worth a dollar, what does a 10% float cut in a day prove?

A redemption burns tokens and returns dollars. Market value falls because fewer tokens remain, not because each token traded at a discount. That is mechanical. It is the opposite of a depeg story. A broken peg would show the price slipping away from $1 while supply stayed put. Here the price held and the supply left.

For readers who treat PYUSD as on-chain cash inside PayPal’s brand, the stake is liquidity and concentration. A consumer-facing dollar token that can lose nearly a tenth of its float in a day is still small next to USDT and USDC. That is why the percentage move lands harder. Less float can tighten inventory for payments, trading, and collateral on Solana and Ethereum, the chains that lost the most. It can also be ordinary plumbing: eligible parties asked for dollars and got them.

Unknowns remain. Dashboards do not say whether the dollars left crypto, rotated into other dollar tokens, or sat waiting for a later mint. They do not split the burns by customer type. Commercial intent is not in the float math.

The peg promise is still the same question it always was. This day’s answer is about how much of that promise left circulation while the dollar print held.

The post PYUSD Supply Drop Wipes $269M in a Day as Peg Holds appeared first on Live Bitcoin News.

title: Grayscale Reveals ‘Compelling Entry Points’ but Data Says No
description:
Key Takeaways Bitcoin fell 17% to $64,000 in November IBIT shed about 28,000 BTC since October 31 USDC circulation fell […]
The post Grayscale Reveals ‘Compelling Entry Points’ but Data Says No appeared first on Coindoo.
fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Bitcoin fell 17% to $64,000 in November
  • IBIT shed about 28,000 BTC since October 31
  • USDC circulation fell from $73B to $67.9B
  • DBS-JPMorgan service moves bank dollars, no crypto

Grayscale Head of Research Zach Pandl published a November 16 note describing Bitcoin’s roughly 17% slide to about $64,000 in the first two weeks of the month, with Grayscale’s market-cap-weighted Crypto Sectors index down about 18% over the same period. His conclusion is that current prices represent “compelling entry points” for medium- and long-term investors because institutional adoption is intact.

The same day, DBS announced a live cross-border service with JPMorgan’s Kinexys that lets institutions move tokenised US-dollar deposits between Singapore and the United States around the clock. Both events count as institutional crypto adoption in the industry’s shorthand. Only one of them involves anyone buying a crypto asset, and it is not the bank launch.

Pandl’s diagnosis, and what it leaves out

Pandl names two primary drivers. The first is stablecoin outflows: USDC supply started contracting in early October, and the decline accelerated after the October 29 Binance hack, which he reads as investors temporarily pulling money out of crypto over security concerns rather than doubt about regulated stablecoins.

The second is spillover from AI equities. Growth portfolios often hold crypto alongside Nvidia and other AI names, so de-risking those books sells both. He adds a structural link: AI and crypto compete for power capacity, and many Bitcoin miners now sell compute to AI firms, so weaker AI investment reaches Bitcoin’s infrastructure layer.

Technical factors did the rest. Bitcoin closed below its 200-day moving average on November 12, a level trend-following funds treat as a sell trigger. Falling prices liquidated leveraged perpetual positions, and much of the selling landed on a weekend when order books are thin. Pandl’s own counterpoint deserves equal weight: he writes that outflows from crypto exchange-traded products contributed slightly but did not look extreme. The fundamentals case rests on institutional adoption of stablecoins and tokenised assets plus persistent demand for alternative stores of value against ongoing deficit spending.

None of that is wrong. It is incomplete. A corporate treasurer adopting blockchain settlement is choosing an operating tool. A fund manager selling Bitcoin is changing a portfolio. The first decision does not offset the second, because they involve different assets. A service can require bank deposits, a dollar stablecoin, a network’s native coin or Bitcoin itself, and each of those creates a different buyer. November’s data lets each one be checked separately.

Tokenised deposits: Bank dollars stay bank dollars

The DBS announcement connects DBS Token Services with Kinexys’s permissioned Blockchain Deposit Account network, with Partior orchestrating settlement. The service handles USD only. Ant International is the first client, using it for real-time treasury management across its entities in both markets. Transfers between the blockchain accounts and conventional demand deposit accounts still pause for three hours on Saturday afternoons, which the banks say they are working to remove.

Every balance in that system is a deposit liability of DBS or JPMorgan. No step in the flow touches BTC, ETH or SOL, and no fee is paid in a public token. The November 2025 framework the two banks announced did envisage JPMorgan deposit tokens on Base, a public Ethereum layer-2, which would have routed some settlement through a public chain. The live service a year later runs on the permissioned network instead. Coindoo’s earlier report on the JPMorgan-DBS launch covers the operational details.

This is the adoption Pandl cites as a favourable trend, and it is real. For a holder of public crypto assets, its value is indirect at best: it normalises blockchain settlement inside regulated banking without adding a single buyer for the tokens those holders own.

Public chains: The fee is the token, and the fee is tiny

Public networks are different in kind because usage has to be paid for in the native asset. Solana’s fee documentation sets the base fee at 5,000 lamports per signature, or 0.000005 SOL, with half burned and half paid to the validator. With SOL trading in the low $80s on November 12, that base fee is worth about four hundredths of a cent. A $10 million USDC transfer with one signature costs the sender a fraction of a cent in SOL plus whatever priority fee they choose to add.

So the mechanism Pandl’s case needs does exist on public chains, but its scale is set by transaction count and congestion, not by the dollar value moved. Circle reported $13.9 trillion of on-chain USDC volume in the third quarter. Almost none of that value had to be converted into a network token to move. Transaction value, transaction count and fee spend are three different numbers, and only the last one is demand for the coin.

READ MORE:

Crypto Traders Can Get 3x Equity Exposure Through Spot Tokens

Bitcoin: What the IBIT share count shows

Bitcoin has no fee mechanism to lean on. Its case is scarcity and store-of-value allocation, which means the only evidence that matters is whether holdings of BTC are rising. A physically backed fund gives the cleanest reading, as long as the right number is used. An IBIT share changing hands on Nasdaq moves no Bitcoin; only the creation or redemption of baskets changes what the trust holds.

The trust’s third-quarter 10-Q reports 1,434,080,000 shares outstanding on October 31. The iShares product page showed 1,384,280,000 on November 16, with each 40,000-share basket backed by 22.64 BTC. That is a net redemption of about 49.8 million shares, or roughly 28,000 BTC leaving the trust in eleven trading days, about 3.5% of the fund.

Put that beside the price. Holdings fell 3.5% while Bitcoin fell 17%. The largest Bitcoin fund in the world was a net seller, which contradicts the idea that institutions were buying the dip through ETFs, but it was not a large enough seller to explain the move. That supports Pandl’s reading that the marginal seller sat in leveraged futures and spot, not in the ETF wrapper. It also means the adoption his thesis relies on, stablecoins and tokenised deposits, produced no measurable Bitcoin purchases during the period he describes.

Stablecoins: The off-ramp claim, tested

Circle’s transparency page reports issuance, redemptions and circulation separately, which makes Pandl’s first driver checkable. Circulation stood at about 73 billion USDC on October 8, 70 billion on October 29 and 67.9 billion on November 12. That is roughly a 7% contraction in five weeks, with the pace quickening after the Binance incident, exactly the pattern Pandl describes. Circle’s own third-quarter average was 73.3 billion, so the November figure sits well below where the quarter ran.

What the data confirms is net redemption: more USDC was handed back to Circle for dollars than was minted. What it cannot show is where those dollars went. A redemption from an exchange treasury rebalancing toward USDT looks identical, on Circle’s page, to an investor leaving crypto. Pandl’s off-ramp reading is consistent with the figures but not proven by them, and Coindoo’s reporting on dip-buying alongside dollar withdrawals shows the two can run together.

The common mistake is to add this contraction to ETF outflows and falling exchange balances and call the sum “capital leaving crypto.” The three series overlap. An investor who redeems USDC to buy IBIT shares from another holder shows up as a stablecoin outflow and nothing else. Each measure answers one question, and they should be read side by side rather than summed.

Confirms the entry-point case

IBIT shares outstanding back above 1.43 billion, its October 31 level, before the trust’s year-end report.

Confirms the entry-point case

USDC circulation reclaiming 70 billion on Circle’s weekly page by mid-December, with issuance outrunning redemptions.

Weakens it

A second straight month of net IBIT redemptions while bank tokenisation headlines continue, which would show adoption and token demand still decoupled.

What could make Grayscale’s case stronger

Pandl’s note is addressed to medium- and long-term investors and does not claim the market has bottomed. The stronger version of his argument is one where adoption reaches the assets being bought: net fund creations that rebuild holdings, sustained public-chain usage with fee demand large enough to matter, and USDC issuance

fullContent:
Another potential bearish news for Bitcoin as it faces another dangerous test after a brutal sell-off pushed BTC toward $62,000, before recovering to $64,000 today. Now, derivatives traders are positioning for another leg lower, with $60,000 emerging as the market’s biggest bearish options bet.

Deribit data shows $900 million in open interest on Bitcoin put options at the $60,000 strike. The position has overtaken the $100,000 call as the exchange’s largest individual options bet.

Wintermute also sees more downside ahead, identifying $60,000 as a potential magnet if Bitcoin loses its recent support levels. Its November 16 market report warned that Bitcoin’s technical breakdown could open the door to prices in the $50,000 range.

Meanwhile, Washington is taking blockchain markets in a very different direction. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has approved new blockchain-based derivatives infrastructure, opening another regulated pathway for digital asset trading in the United States.

Market Cap

Bitcoin Bears Circle $60,000 as Deribit Put Options Surge

Bitcoin’s latest decline has changed the mood across derivatives markets. The $100,000 call, previously the largest options position on Deribit, has lost its crown to the $60,000 put. According to data, the $60,000 put carries $900 million in notional open interest. The $100,000 call follows closely with $867 million.

The shift shows a dramatic change in market positioning. Traders who previously concentrated on Bitcoin’s recovery toward six figures are now watching how much further the crypto could fall. Yet the change only shows that traders are closing bullish positions rather than simply rushing into bearish bets.

Bitcoin fell 12.7% to $65,400, closing below its 200-week moving average at $68,000. It briefly touched $62,000 over the weekend, marking its lowest level since July. For now, $62,000 is the first important downside level, followed by the $60,000 options cluster. A sustained breakdown could expose Bitcoin to further losses into the $50,000 range.

The derivatives market is already showing signs of stress. Bitcoin’s 30-day implied volatility index surged to 57.13, its highest reading since June, as traders rushed to protect their positions.

In Bitcoin news today, the $60,000 level is becoming increasingly important. A move toward that price could force traders to reassess their exposure just as market confidence deteriorates.

DISCOVER: 15+ Upcoming Coinbase Listings to Watch in 2026

CFTC Approves Blockchain Derivatives Exchanges in Major US Shift

While Bitcoin bears are preparing for another difficult stretch, American regulators are opening new doors for blockchain-based financial markets. Last night UK time, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig announced approvals for new derivatives infrastructure involving Backpack and tZERO.

Backpack is coming home to the USA.

We’ve received landmark CFTC approval to establish the first-ever derivatives exchange powered by one order book with unified global liquidity.

Leveraged perpetuals. Crypto collateral. Cross-margin. 24/7 trading.

Join the waitlist:…

— Backpack (@Backpack) November 16, 2026

Backpack received approval to establish a US derivatives exchange and derivatives clearing organization. The licenses provide the regulatory foundation for its planned US trading operations. The platform intends to offer crypto perpetual futures with leverage, 24-hour trading, crypto collateral, and cross-margin capabilities through a unified order book.

tZERO also received its exchange approval last week, following an earlier authorization to operate a derivatives clearing organization.

Together, these developments mark an important step toward bringing blockchain-based derivatives trading under established US financial oversight.

Derivatives are already a major part of crypto price discovery. Bringing more trading infrastructure onshore could eventually attract additional institutional participation.

DISCOVER: 15+ Best Crypto IPO to Watch in 2026

Bitcoin Price Weakness and Its Bearish News Contrast With Growing Blockchain Adoption Today

The timing creates an interesting contradiction for the crypto market. Bitcoin is struggling to maintain support as traders increasingly protect themselves against another major decline. Yet blockchain-based financial infrastructure is gaining regulatory acceptance in the world’s largest financial market.

A recovery above the $68,000 200-week moving average would help challenge the bearish outlook. Until then, the $62,000 low and the $60,000 options strike remain critical levels.

Bitcoin’s next move could determine if this correction becomes another buying opportunity or the beginning of a much deeper market downturn.

title: a16z 的傲慢与偏见
description:
Chainfeeds 导读：

一家精通讲故事的 VC，被困在了自己的故事里。

文章来源：

https://foresightnews.pro/article/detail/101687

文章作者：

Foresight News

观点：

Foresight News：a16z 至今投资了 154 个 Web3 项目，这些项目的总融资额达到 206 亿美元。154 个项目仅占所有获得融资 Web3 项目总数的约 2.5%，但 206 亿美元却占到了总融资额的超 13%。其中，对 Coinbase 的 2 亿美元投资让 a16z 获得了约 70 亿美元的现金回报。这个案例成为 a16z 后续募资路演 PPT 中的常客。在 154 个项目中，按照巅峰期估值或币价计算，让 a16z 获得超 50 倍纸面回报的项目占比至少超过了 10%。单单在 DeFi 领域，DefiLlama 上 TVL 数据排名前 11 的 DeFi 项目中，a16z 投资的项目就有 5 个。在 DefiLlama 统计的 7002 个 DeFi 项目中，这 5 个项目在数量上占比不到千分之一，但拿走了 DeFi 总 TVL 的至少 30%。a16z 投资了 Solana、Sui、Avalanche 和 NEAR 等公链，Solana 和 Sui 属于本轮周期中少有的表现突出的项目；在 DeFi 领域，Lido、Morpho、EigenCloud、Sky 和 Uniswap 均进入 TVL 排名前 11 的项目之列。Optimism 则通过其 Rollup 堆栈支持 Coinbase 的 L2 Base、Kraken 的 L2 Ink 以及 Uniswap 的 Unichain 等独立 L2。OpenSea 在 2022 年初估值一度达到 133 亿美元，Yuga Labs 旗下 BAYC 系列 NFT 曾成为明星追捧的社交名片，巅峰时期单枚价值高达数百万人民币。 早期行业的核心矛盾是缺乏共识，资本不敢进入、人才不敢加入、监管难以理解。这一阶段，能够将复杂技术转化为市场故事的机构，实际上承担了市场教育功能。在 DeFi Summer 和 NFT 浪潮中，叙事能力帮助行业完成冷启动，将资本、注意力和创业者快速聚集起来。NFT 曾被视为实现真正数字所有权的关键原语，使艺术、音乐、游戏道具等资产能够由用户真正拥有并跨平台流通；链游围绕玩家资产所有权、Play-to-Earn 和开放经济展开；元宇宙则强调开放、去中心化、用户控制身份以及价值归用户所有。然而，后续市场发展并未完全按照这一设想进行，Web3 行业快速进入下行期，DeFi 因为拥有大量实际应用场景而复苏，NFT 等新概念却逐渐失去市场关注。游戏、NFT、社交、DePIN、创作者经济等赛道，在短期内难以实现规模化以及与市场需求的契合。EigenLayer 的再质押模式通过将 ETH 流动性质押代币作为其他网络共识节点的抵押品，为新网络提供共享安全保障，但再质押服务实际支付的费用始终无法覆盖基础质押收益与风险溢价，额外收益几乎从未真正兑现。2025 年惩罚措施上线后，风险从理论变成可定价，ether.fi 等主力流动性再质押协议因缺乏实质收益而大举撤离。 Story Protocol 试图将知识产权转化为链上可编程资产，上线之初就有多个音乐版权领域的项目入驻，其中部分项目也获得了融资。但传统版权方缺乏上链动力，真实授权与链上登记之间始终存在鸿沟，链上收入长期接近于零，实际使用场景与市场预期严重脱节。项目最后一轮私募融资估值达到 22.5 亿美元，但后续发展未能匹配这一估值。近期，项目改名 DATA，将叙事从「可编程 IP」转向「AI 训练数据」，并考虑关停自有链。在宣布关停 L1 时，Story Protocol 的链上 TVL 已从巅峰时期的超过 4500 万美元跌至约 300 万美元，9 月链上手续费收入不足 4000 美元，不到前一年同期 14.5 万美元的零头。EigenLayer 和 Story Protocol 的发展经历反映出一个共同问题：宏大叙事先于真实需求，供给侧的技术与代币故事发展迅速，但需求侧的付费和实际使用始终未能跟上。与此同时，2024 年开始，许多投资机构逐渐转向稳定币、支付和 RWA 代币化等方向，但 a16z 在支付和稳定币两个赛道仅投资了 9 个项目，在其投资组合中的占比不到 6%，RWA 代币化方向则没有投资项目。宏观经济下行也改变了一级市场的投资环境，利率、流动性和风险偏好决定了市场愿意为故事支付多少溢价。当市场进入下行周期，新概念的边际回报急剧缩水，叙事推高估值、估值兑现回报的正反馈随之中断，留下的是高位接盘者的亏损。

Alea Research：HYPE 在六周内经历了双重估值下降：一方面是代币价格下跌，另一方面是 Assistance Fund 资金流入增加。HYPE 于 11 月 9 日收于 75.10 美元，较 9 月 30 日下跌 17.5%。Hyperliquid 的手续费收入会流入 Assistance Fund，该基金使用资金回购 HYPE，并将其视为已销毁代币。10 月 1 日至 11 月 9 日，Assistance Fund 日均流入达到 221 万美元，较第三季度日均水平增长 20.2%。其中，大部分增量来自 Coinbase 的 USDC 储备收益分成，该收入机制于 8 月 26 日开始计入；同期，仅计算交易手续费带来的资金流入，增幅只有 2.4%。HYPE 完全稀释估值与 Assistance Fund 过去 92 天年化资金流入的比率，从 9 月 30 日的 135.7 倍降至 11 月 9 日的 89.6 倍。其中，HYPE 价格下跌使该倍数减少 23.7 倍，资金流入增长则使其进一步减少 22.4 倍。10 月，USDC 储备收益占 Assistance Fund 总流入的 23.8%，高于第三季度的 10.5%。按照 11 月 9 日的收入速度计算，这部分收益年化约为 1.89 亿美元。第四季度截至 11 月 9 日，Assistance Fund 日均回购 26,704 枚 HYPE，高于第三季度的 24,775 枚，增长约 7.8%。 11 月前 9 天，Hyperliquid 永续合约日均交易量达到 98.9 亿美元，较第三季度平均水平增长 27%。其中，HIP-3 市场交易量占比达到 43.8%，为 7 月以来最高水平，交易量中约 98% 来自 trade [XYZ]，主要包括 XYZ100 指数、标普 500 指数和 SK hynix 市场。随着 HIP-3 市场占比提高，Assistance Fund 从每美元交易额中获得的手续费分成有所下降。自 7 月以来，每当 HIP-3 交易量占比提高 10 个百分点，基金每美元交易额的收入分成就会下降约 0.27 个基点。没有 HIP-3 交易量时，基金每美元交易额的收入分成约为 3.05 个基点，这也是核心市场支付的水平。Hyperliquid 的手续费机制规定，处于增长模式的 HIP-3 市场，协议手续费降至正常费率的十分之一，而部署方可以在此基础上收取自己的费用。增长模式能够帮助部署方通过降低交易成本吸引更多交易量，但也会减少协议每笔交易获得的收入。如果按照 11 月的交易速度，将 10 个百分点的交易量从核心市场转移至 HIP-3 市场，Assistance Fund 年收入将减少约 9700 万美元。与此同时，trade [XYZ] 的增长模式将部署方自身的手续费分成限制在基础费率的 100%，而非增长模式下最高可达到 300%；每次切换模式后，相关市场还会锁定 30 天。 Assistance Fund 目前拥有两类收入来源：一类是交易者支付的手续费，另一类是 Coinbase 根据 Hyperliquid 上 USDC 储备产生的收益支付的分成。根据 Hyperliquid 的报价资产规则，Coinbase 每 30 天向 Assistance Fund 支付相关 USDC 背后美国国债净收益的约 90%。这是因为未来一次协议升级将允许只有符合规则的稳定币作为 Hyperliquid 主要永续合约市场的报价资产。Coinbase 的第二笔款项为 1592 万美元，于 11 月 3 日到账。截至 11 月 9 日，Hyperliquid 上的 USDC 规模为 65.3 亿美元，较 9 月 30 日下降 12%。每次美联储降息 25 个基点，预计每年将使这部分收入减少约 1500 万美元。Coinbase 还需要质押 50 万枚 HYPE，如果支付不足，验证者可以对其进行罚没；如果停止支付，则必须提前六个月通知。下一笔款项预计于 12 月 3 日左右支付，截至 11 月 11 日的累计应计金额约为 1540 万美元。与此同时，Assistance Fund 第三季度收入为 1.691 亿美元，第四季度截至 11 月 9 日已达到 8840 万美元。若要超过第三季度，11 月和 12 月平均每月需要获得 5010 万美元收入，较 10 月低 27%。在当前 1.68 个基点的手续费分成水平下，剩余时间内永续合约日均交易量需要达到 62 亿美元。若手续费分成下降至 1.4 个基点，则日均交易量门槛将提高至 74 亿美元。美国市场的交易量还需要等待 HIP-3* 主网上线及 CFTC 对相关参与方的批准。【原文为英文】

title: 【英文】比特币跌势背后：ETF 撤资、杠杆出清与短期持有者的集体亏损
description:
Chainfeeds 导读：

市场杠杆已得到集中出清，但 ETF 资金仍持续流出，短期持有者普遍陷入亏损，投资者止损离场规模达到 7 月以来最高水平。

文章来源：

https://research.glassnode.com/btc-market-pulse-week-47-2026/

文章作者：

glassnode

观点：

glassnode：比特币周一在 6.4 万美元附近交易，此前一周收跌约 13%。本轮下跌始于周四，并在周末进一步加速，期间 BTC 一度跌破 6.3 万美元，周六收盘价创下 8 月中旬以来新低。价格动能跌破低位区间，现货和永续合约市场的主动卖方均大幅增加，推动两项累计成交量差（CVD）指标跌破各自低位区间，同时现货成交量升至高位区间上方。此次抛售清理了市场此前积累的大量杠杆。期货未平仓合约量降至区间底部，较七天前下降 7.2%，从 369 亿美元降至 342 亿美元，创 8 月以来最低水平。多头资金费支付额下降 29.4%，从 280 万美元降至 200 万美元，此前连续数周处于高位区间，如今已回落至正常范围。永续合约累计成交量差降至负 14 亿美元，较七天前的负 4.93 亿美元进一步恶化，反映杠杆交易者在下跌过程中持续主动卖出。期权市场方面，25 Delta 偏度升至 13.7%，高于高位区间，创 8 月以来最高水平，看跌期权相较看涨期权的溢价进一步扩大，显示交易者正在增加下行保护需求。 美国现货比特币 ETF 投资者持续减仓，过去一周每个交易日均出现资金净流出，周度净流出约 9.954 亿美元，虽然较前一周的 11 亿美元有所收窄，但机构需求依然疲弱。美国现货 BTC ETF 交易量从 129 亿美元下降 11.2% 至 115 亿美元，处于近期区间较低水平，表明 ETF 投资者在价格下跌期间持续降低敞口，而非集中恐慌性离场。与此同时，ETF MVRV 从 1.28 下降 16.9% 至 1.06，跌破低位区间并接近 1.0 的盈亏平衡水平，即平均 ETF 持有者的持仓成本附近。此次下跌几乎耗尽了基金投资者此前积累的账面利润，使高位买入的投资者面临更大压力。链上活动仍然活跃，实体调整后的转账量升至 54 亿美元，接近高位区间，日活跃地址数达到 65.97 万个，仍高于高位区间。这表明市场并未因价格下跌而陷入沉寂，大量比特币仍在不同实体之间转移，资金正在重新配置，投资者在更低价格水平上持续进行资产交换。与此同时，月度已实现市值变化从 0.43% 大幅下降 91% 至 0.04%，表明过去一个月的新增资金流入几乎消失，进入网络的资金已不足以抵消亏损卖出的代币。 本轮下跌的损失主要由近期买入者承担。短期持有者目前平均处于亏损状态，其净未实现盈亏指标从 0.9% 降至负 7.4%，创 7 月以来最低水平，意味着近期买入比特币的投资者平均持仓成本已经高于当前市场价格。短期持有者与长期持有者的供应量比率升至 15.1%，创 3 月以来最高水平，表明新买入者在比特币流通供应中的占比持续增加，更多筹码掌握在对价格变化更加敏感的投资者手中。过去三个月内买入的代币占已实现市值的 22%，同样创 3 月以来最高水平，这部分近期资金在价格下跌期间可能形成更大的抛售压力。当前处于盈利状态的比特币供应量比例从 60.4% 降至 55.3%，创 8 月以来最低水平，意味着仅略高于一半的比特币供应仍处于盈利状态。已实现盈亏比进一步降至负 1.28，跌破低位区间，亏损转移的比特币数量远超盈利转移的数量，创 7 月初以来最低水平。短期持有者的已实现亏损也达到 7 月以来最大水平，反映高位买入的投资者正在承受明显压力。不过，期货未平仓合约和资金费率已经回落，市场此前积累的大量杠杆得到清理，价格动能也进入深度超卖区域。【原文为英文】

Castle Capital

观点：

Castle Capital：加密市场的资金和收入高度集中。过去 12 个月，剔除稳定币发行商后，收入最高的 10 个协议占据了全行业 47% 的协议收入，而代币持有者获得的回报更加集中，排名前 10 的协议占据了 73%。过去 12 个月，加密协议在各个类别中合计创造了 137 亿美元收入，各类别排名前两位的协议至少获得了 52% 的手续费收入，其中稳定币发行商、预测市场、基差交易和期权等类别的头部协议占比超过 90%。不过，并非所有类别都具有相同的集中度。Launchpad 和现货 DEX 的竞争更加激烈，用户切换平台的成本较低，交易者更关注最优交易路径和最低成本，因此交易流量会分散到不同平台。借贷和永续合约 DEX 则更加依赖激励和流动性，优惠激励能够吸引资金，而充足的流动性有助于头部协议维持竞争优势。协议收入增长也不意味着代币一定表现良好，代币持有者实际获得的收入、代币增发带来的稀释，以及市场对未来增长的预期，都会影响代币表现。Uniswap 和 Hyperliquid 过去 12 个月的持有者收入估值有所下降，而其他代币则变得更加昂贵。Derive 是估值最高的代币，其价格更多反映未来增长预期；PUMP 则是估值最低的代币之一，虽然拥有持续现金流，但产品依赖投机性 Memecoin 活动，市场情绪尚未明显改善。 DeFi 和代币化资产所面对的潜在市场规模以万亿美元计，对于目前的头部协议而言，现有收入仍只是整体市场的一小部分。Hyperliquid 年化手续费收入已经达到约 8.95 亿美元，相当于 CME 约 55 亿美元年化清算及交易手续费收入的 16%。目前 Hyperliquid 仍受到美国监管限制，尚未向美国用户开放，但这一情况正在发生变化。纽约证券交易所母公司 ICE 已与 TradeXYZ 合作并进行投资，计划在 Hyperliquid 上推出涵盖加密货币、股票、大宗商品和外汇的美国永续合约市场。Kraken 母公司 Payward 也通过旗下 Bitnomial Exchange 和 NinjaTrader Clearing，成为首个受 CFTC 监管的 HIP-3 部署方。Uniswap 则在现货 DEX 市场占据领先地位，过去 30 天交易量占比约 25%，过去 12 个月手续费收入占比约 31%。其 2026 年下半年收入增长主要来自代币化资产和 Robinhood 相关活动。现实世界资产规模今年以来从约 250 亿美元增长至约 400 亿美元，McKinsey 预计到 2030 年，代币化资产市场规模可能达到 2 万亿美元。随着更多代币化资产进入链上交易，DEX 能够提供全天候流动性，成为相关市场的重要交易基础设施。Uniswap V4 的 Hooks 架构还允许开发者创建具有权限限制的资金池，为受到转让限制的资产提供交易支持。 Pendle 的增长与现实世界资产代币化密切相关。截至 2026 年第三季度末，由现实世界资产支持的美元市场占 Pendle 总锁仓价值的 82%，第三季度 TVL 增长 43%。相关市场包括 Agora 和 Global Dollar 发行的美债支持型美元、Re Protocol 的再保险资产，以及 USDAi 提供的 GPU 抵押贷款。每一种新的生息型现实世界资产都需要 Pendle 市场提供更好的分发能力和 DeFi 可组合性，随着代币化资产规模扩大，Pendle 有望从中受益。目前 Pendle 的 TVL 约为 10 亿美元，如果其在持续增长的 RWA 市场中占据 10% 的份额，每年可向持有者支付超过 4300 万美元。Aave 则处于代币化资产、消费级应用和核心 DeFi 的交汇点，目前拥有约 120 亿美元活跃贷款，今年迄今收入达到 6100 万美元。随着借贷规模扩大，平台收入也有望同步增长。与此同时，Venice AI 提供私密、无审查的模型访问服务，作为 Claude 和 ChatGPT 的替代选择，其年化收入达到 1.23 亿美元。Venice 通过自主和自动回购机制向 VVV 代币持有者回馈部分收入，过去 30 天回购销毁金额达到 102 万美元，折合年化约 1219 万美元。Zcash 则代表另一种以未来需求为核心的投资逻辑，其网络收入相对较低，但隐私功能正在获得更多使用，过去三年隐私保护状态下的 ZEC 占比从 8% 上升至 29.2%。Grayscale 的 Zcash ETF 自 8 月 25 日开始交易以来，吸引超过 10 亿美元资金流入。

title: Bitcoin muted at $65.2k as crypto sentiment dithers, ETF outflows persist
Crypto Market Value Jumped 40% in Q3, but Retail Spot Trading Didn’t Follow
description:
eToro's funded user accounts jumped 18% over the past year, yet its clients placed 62% fewer crypto trades this October than a year earlier. That disconnect captures the paradox of the third quarter: crypto prices staged 40% rebound, but the retail spot trading volumes did not. 
Across major centralised platforms, spot trading turnover contracted by 14.2% sequentially in Q3, while direct crypto execution on mainstream consumer platforms remained in a deep slump compared to 2025.
Crypto market capitalisation rose 39.6% from Q2 to Q3. Broker disclosures, meanwhile, showed lower direct crypto trading activity than a year earlier:
Bitcoin ETF Inflows Returned as Spot Trading Stayed Weak 
With trading revenues pressured on venues like Coinbase and Robinhood, retail capital has increasingly bypassed direct spot tokens entirely, diverting instead into spot ETFs, leveraged perpetuals, and booming prediction markets.
US spot bitcoin ETFs took in $6.34 billion of net inflows in Q3, according to SoSoValue data, after roughly $5 billion of outflows in the second quarter. As those purchases are trades in fund shares, they do not appear in a broker’s direct crypto trading figures. 
Earlier in the year, institutions accounted for 72% of spot volume on Wintermute’s OTC desk, up from 59% a year earlier. The firm described a market “with retail largely absent and preoccupied with equities.” 
 Trading Platforms Expand Beyond Crypto Spot 
Prediction market volume reached a record $188 billion in Q3, 21 times the level a year earlier, according to CryptoRank.  Much of Kalshi's September growth is linked to sports-linked combinations. 
At Robinhood, prediction markets have out-earned crypto for two quarters in a row. At Coinbase, prediction markets and derivatives together now account for about a quarter of transaction revenue. 
Derivatives also took a larger share of exchange activity as spot turnover fell. They accounted for 83% of total exchange volume in Q3, according to TokenInsight. Separately, open interest on perpetual futures rose 40.6% over the quarter to more than $100 billion.
The Market Remained Below Its 2025 Level 
The Q3 rally followed three consecutive quarters of decline in crypto market capitalisation. Bitcoin had lost about a third of its value between January and June. Total crypto market value closed September at $2.96 trillion, still 4% down for the year. 
According to Coingecko reports, ayear earlier it stood at $4 trillion, while bitcoin ended September 2025 near $114,000, compared with about $83,500 this September.  
The third quarter confirmed that the traditional retail crypto playbook has fractured. In previous cycles, a 40% market surge would have triggered record onboarding and retail churn. In 2026, user bases grew, but transactions languished as capital migrated into ETFs, prediction markets, and perpetuals. 
Incoming fourth-quarter trading data will show whether retail investors were simply late to the rebound or whether the spot trading appetite has structurally cooled. 


This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

eToro's funded user accounts jumped 18% over the past year, yet its clients placed 62% fewer crypto trades this October than a year earlier. That disconnect captures the paradox of the third quarter: crypto prices staged 40% rebound, but the retail spot trading volumes did not.

Across major centralised platforms, spot trading turnover contracted by 14.2% sequentially in Q3, while direct crypto execution on mainstream consumer platforms remained in a deep slump compared to 2025.

Crypto market capitalisation rose 39.6% from Q2 to Q3. Broker disclosures, meanwhile, showed lower direct crypto trading activity than a year earlier:

Bitcoin ETF Inflows Returned as Spot Trading Stayed Weak

With trading revenues pressured on venues like Coinbase and Robinhood, retail capital has increasingly bypassed direct spot tokens entirely, diverting instead into spot ETFs, leveraged perpetuals, and booming prediction markets.

US spot bitcoin ETFs took in $6.34 billion of net inflows in Q3, according to SoSoValue data, after roughly $5 billion of outflows in the second quarter. As those purchases are trades in fund shares, they do not appear in a broker’s direct crypto trading figures.

Earlier in the year, institutions accounted for 72% of spot volume on Wintermute’s OTC desk, up from 59% a year earlier. The firm described a market “with retail largely absent and preoccupied with equities.”

Trading Platforms Expand Beyond Crypto Spot

Prediction market volume reached a record $188 billion in Q3, 21 times the level a year earlier, according to CryptoRank. Much of Kalshi's September growth is linked to sports-linked combinations.

At Robinhood, prediction markets have out-earned crypto for two quarters in a row. At Coinbase, prediction markets and derivatives together now account for about a quarter of transaction revenue.

Derivatives also took a larger share of exchange activity as spot turnover fell. They accounted for 83% of total exchange volume in Q3, according to TokenInsight. Separately, open interest on perpetual futures rose 40.6% over the quarter to more than $100 billion.

The Market Remained Below Its 2025 Level

The Q3 rally followed three consecutive quarters of decline in crypto market capitalisation. Bitcoin had lost about a third of its value between January and June. Total crypto market value closed September at $2.96 trillion, still 4% down for the year.

According to Coingecko reports, ayear earlier it stood at $4 trillion, while bitcoin ended September 2025 near $114,000, compared with about $83,500 this September.

The third quarter confirmed that the traditional retail crypto playbook has fractured. In previous cycles, a 40% market surge would have triggered record onboarding and retail churn. In 2026, user bases grew, but transactions languished as capital migrated into ETFs, prediction markets, and perpetuals.

Incoming fourth-quarter trading data will show whether retail investors were simply late to the rebound or whether the spot trading appetite has structurally cooled.

This article was written by Tanya Chepkova at www.financemagnates.com.

title: Jeffrey Epstein's death may not have been suicide, new analysis suggests
description:
Warning: This article and video contain graphic images that may be disturbing.
Across the political spectrum, a large chunk of Americans believe, despite a lack of evidence, that Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide.
Now one forensics expert, working with photos and files provided by Epstein's brother, is weighing in to contend that this suspicion might be right. 
Dr. Michael Freeman, who is editor-in-chief of the Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine, spent months reviewing never-before-published autopsy records provided to him and CBS News by Epstein's brother. The 2019 ruling by the New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner was that Epstein died by suicide. But Freeman has concluded that Epstein's death was more likely a homicide. 
Freeman — who worked with Anders Eriksson, a professor of forensic medicine at Umea University in Sweden, and Itiel Dror, a researcher specializing in identifying bias in forensic decision making — presented their findings Monday in London. Freeman said he believes that in August 2019 the world's most notorious sex abuser was likely attacked and killed by another person. 
"The injuries that were documented by the medical examiner were not consistent with the suicidal hanging. And the injuries that were attributed to something other than potentially a physical struggle or assault were just overlooked," Freeman told CBS News, based on his review of the autopsy records, photos and a biomedical reconstruction he produced.
The report is the second by an outside forensic expert to question the official findings of suicide. In 2020, Epstein's brother hired forensic pathologist Dr. Michael Baden to look into the death, as first reported by "60 Minutes." At the time, Baden said injuries to Epstein's neck raised doubts about the official ruling. He told "60 Minutes" the evidence he saw pointed more to murder than suicide.
Freeman's report was rejected for publication from an academic journal, he acknowledged. He said reviewers for the journal thought it wasn't appropriate to criticize a medical examiner's findings in a peer-reviewed publication. Freeman plans to resubmit, he said.
Freeman, a professor of forensic medicine, said he was struck by the first image he examined, depicting the right side of Epstein's upper body and face, with ligature wounds visible on his neck.
"When I saw this photograph, my first reaction was that that is a very unusual looking injury for a hanging on the neck," Freeman said.

Freeman has testified as a forensic expert in high-profile court cases and was a member of the Maryland attorney general's audit team that reviewed dozens of in-custody deaths last year.  Still, forensic pathology is not an exact science. Credible experts often interpret the same evidence very differently. Neck injuries from hanging or strangulation can be especially ambiguous. And Epstein's death investigation was marked by added uncertainty because of a cascade of blunders in the hours, days and weeks after his body was discovered in his Manhattan federal jail cell.  
The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner — which conducted the autopsy on Aug. 11, 2019, the day after Epstein was found dead — declined an interview request, and did not reply directly to Freeman's findings when pressed by CBS News.  
"Our office stands by its determination," a spokesperson for the medical examiner said.
There has been support for that finding. In June, The New York Times conducted an investigation that it said relied on tens of thousands of pages of newly released documents, as well as Epstein's own notes handwritten in jail. That report said there were indications Epstein was intent on ending his own life. And the newspaper reported that, of the forensics experts they interviewed, "almost none of them believed that his manner of death  — suicide or homicide — could be conclusively settled based on the medical evidence alone."
"That's not what suicidal hangings do"
Freeman believes the official investigation missed key details.
"The injury pattern was described as a sloped or as a peaked injury that was a perfect description for a hanging. But that's not what we saw when we saw the photos," Freeman said.
While one mark fit that description, he noticed a second mark in the ligature wounds on Epstein's neck, beneath and angled differently than the mark above it.
"There is no mechanism to produce a second mark that would be lower. Even if the ligature was tied with two loops, both loops would go up to the point where it was tied because that's the anchor point," Freeman said.
Asked if the two markings, present on each side of Epstein's neck, could have been indicative of him stopping and starting — trying twice to kill himself — Freeman said available research into suicidal hanging indicates that's unlikely. Epstein would have had to make "a false start that was strong enough to break his hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage and give him a deep abrasion and then maintain consciousness," Freeman said. 
It's an explanation that doesn't make sense, he said.
"That's not what suicidal hangings do," Freeman said. "The body becomes unconscious and then it is the weight of the body that produces the abrasion, not any kind of running jump at it. That opportunity really isn't there. That's not a realistic scenario for any hanging described in any of the literature throughout the world."
None of the prison guards on duty when Epstein died spoke to medical examiner investigators, according to Justice Department records. Some of them falsified records and lied about their activities the night before and morning of Epstein's death. Corrections officer Michael Thomas is credited with finding Epstein's body. He only agreed to be interviewed by investigators after he was charged with crimes two years later. 
There's no indication that the medical examiner's office revisited its determination after Thomas agreed to share his account. Freeman, however, based his reconstruction of the scene of Epstein's death on Thomas' later description, in which he said he found Epstein hanging from a bedpost.
Freeman constructed a biomechanical analysis, or series of three-dimensional models, based on Thomas' description of the scene, as well as wounds and abrasions visible in images of Epstein's body.

"The biomechanical analysis was designed to be able to map the injuries on a model that was…as close to the anatomy and size and shape of Epstein as possible," Freeman said. 
The 3-D model allowed Freeman to test the suicide hypothesis. What the model showed is that some of the abrasions and injuries visible on Epstein's neck were indicative of suicidal hanging, but some on his neck, and elsewhere on his body including an injury to his shoulder, weren't.
"We have too many other injuries that are not explained by any suicidal hanging. Because I don't care how this guy is found, where did these other injuries come from?" Freeman asked. "How do you get the deep soft tissue hemorrhage in his left shoulder? How do you get the injury on his back?" 
His conclusion will add fuel to the fire of conspiracy theories that have consumed much of the popular discourse around Epstein's death.
The alternate theory: Strangulation
"The alternative scenario is that there was a strangulation that occurred," Freeman said. In particular, horizontal marks on Epstein's neck point to ligature being pulled from behind him, he said. 
Epstein's cell was littered with piles of torn orange fabric, the bedding used in cells at the Manhattan Correctional Center. Freeman says an image shows one knotted fabric that he believes appears to support the strangulation theory.

"That is a double knotted, looped, narrow ligature that was found in the cell that was dropped in a corner near the desk. And if we put those together in a format in which the knot, one of these knots, is applied as pressure to produce this irregular abrasion at the back of the neck, we actually have a fairly good explanation for all the injuries," Freeman said.
He also noticed what he claims are signs of an assault and struggle, including blunt force trauma to the face and the left shoulder.
"And we see what appeared to be consistent with fingernail marks above the ligature," Freeman said. "And if you put it all together, it is most consistent with a homicidal strangulation from behind using a narrow knotted fabric ligature."
The fabric Freeman believes matches Epstein's injuries wasn't collected for the medical examiner. 
"What you see in this front view of the ligature pattern is that it is ragged looking," Freeman said, referring to the markings on Epstein's neck. "It is segmented looking. It's not smooth. This certainly would not be consistent with the noose that was taken from the room." 
Epstein's death drew global headlines and promises from the top levels of the Justice Department that it would be among the most scrutinized inmate deaths in history. Instead, it was marked by a series of failures.
A flawed investigation?
The issues with Epstein's death scene began almost immediately on Aug. 10, 2019. 
Thomas reported finding Epstein's body, cold to the touch, around 6:30 a.m. 
"The fact that to touch, Epstein's body was cold, would indicate he had been dead for at least a few hours," Freeman said. 
Epstein's body was moved out of the cell within minutes of being discovered, preventing accurate photography of the scene when investigators first arrived that day. The cell was never sealed off for forensic investigation, and much of the evidence at the scene wasn't properly preserved, a 2025 CBS News investigation found. 
To make matters worse, most of the closed-circuit cameras in Epstein's wing of the prison were not functioning. And Justice Department documents show investigators who reviewed footage from the nearest working camera — one that looked over a common area connecting multiple tiers of cells — did not follow up on some details, including an unexplained orange blur seen ascending a staircase toward Epstein's block the night of his death. 
It took two years for federal investigators to interview Thomas, who had been charged with lying and falsifying prison records, and provided a statement in exchange for leniency. It took another year for those same investigators to talk to the medical examiner who examined Epstein's body. 
And Freeman said the medical examiner may have misinterpreted key details on Epstein's body. She noted that there were no broken fingernails or defensive wounds on the hands. An abrasion on Epstein's arm was probably from convulsing during hanging, the medical examiner said.
"When she talks about the fact that there's only a little scratch on the arm, she completely overlooks the fact that there was deep intramuscular hemorrhage in the left shoulder that was undoubtedly due to blunt force trauma," Freeman said.
To Freeman, the mystery of Epstein's death is not how he died, but who killed him. 
"I'm comfortable saying that's a mystery. Who did it? Exactly how they did it. What happened? All the other things. Why the cameras [were] off? All a mystery, yes," Freeman said. "Was this a suicide? Not a mystery."

The New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner — which conducted the autopsy on Aug. 11, 2019, the day after Epstein was found dead — declined an interview request, and did not reply directly to Freeman's findings when pressed by CBS News.

title: Meet the Researcher: Madelyne Xiao
description:

The post Meet the Researcher: Madelyne Xiao appeared first on CITP Blog.
fullContent:
Pictured: Madelyne Xiao (left), Jason Persaud ’27 (right)

Jason Persaud: I’ll start with a basic intro: could you tell us a little bit about your work and the research you do?

Madelyne Xiao: I’m broadly interested in online speech and identity, but also the media and how news is made. That includes what happens in the newsroom, on-the-ground reporting, and the security of sources during investigative, primary-source reporting.

I use a mix of techniques, including user and measurement studies. More recently, I’ve been working with my collaborator at CMU, Sarah Scheffler, using applied cryptography to develop pipelines for private analytics on encrypted messaging. Depending on the day, I might be doing human-factors research or more “applied-crypto-flavored” things. It’s all with an eye toward understanding how people represent themselves online, and how offline values—like polarity and authenticity—translate to digital identity.

Jason: That’s really cool. Your path to where you are now involved a lot of journalism, fact-checking, and science writing, but now you’re in computer science research. What inspired you to study the information ecosystem from a technical perspective?

Madelyne: The fact-checking role was probably the most instrumental. I worked in The New Yorker’s fact-checking department, which is a very particular place to work. I don’t think anything quite like it exists in any other media outlet.

Working on a daily website and a weekly magazine, we were trying to do labor-intensive checking at scale with a relatively small crew. 

As a first-year grad student working with my adviser, Jonathan Mayer, I investigated automated fact-checking systems. I was immediately struck by the disconnect between what I understood fact-checking to be and what academic ML and computational linguistics researchers thought it was: there was a level of reductionism required in the academic interpretation to make the problem small enough for a machine learning classifier to handle. 

So much of manual fact-checking is context-building, relationship management, and on-the-fly research. In the academic ML literature, by contrast, fact-checking is more commonly formulated as an information retrieval problem. Coming from a journalism background, where I did this work manually for a long time, I felt that this wasn’t a representative formulation of such a gnarly problem. It’s not just an information problem; it implicates reader bias, the outlet’s reputation, and so much more. These conceptions of “fact-checking”were worlds apart.

Soon after I concluded the fact-checking work, I realized that many problems applied cryptographers work on—like encrypted messaging and source security—would be fascinating to journalists. These two groups don’t talk much. Tools developed by cryptographers are often cool in theory but nearly impossible for a busy journalist to use. Most journalists are more worried about their next gig or keeping up with the news cycle. They want an easy, out-of-the-box tool. Designing for an audience that needs these tools but has limited bandwidth to understand the “how” behind them is a very interesting problem space.

Jason: You mentioned applied cryptography. Is that a project you’re currently working on?

Madelyne: That’s been on the back burner a bit because some age-verification work has taken priority, but I’ve worked on it with Sarah for the past two years — we’ve been designing and testing a tool for performing private analytics on encrypted WhatsApp messages (we’ve been describing it as Google Trends for encrypted texts).

Jason: Would you like to talk about a project you’re currently focused on?

Madelyne: Sure, I can give you two. First, with Jonathan and Manoel, I’ve been auditing the Community Notes platform on Twitter (or X). We’ve been at it for over two years, which makes it a bit of a dinosaur in computer science terms. We spent over a year just collecting the cumulative data dumps the platform releases every 24 hours.

We wanted to understand the platform on its own terms—running the algorithm to see how polarity scores correlate with the notes actually published. Now, we’re in a phase where we’re asking Community Notes users about their political preferences to see how those offline notions interact with their activity on the platform.

The second project is the age verification work. There’s a lot of talk in the U.S., U.K., E.U., and Australia about “age gates.” We’re specifically interested in biometric approaches to age verification. To verify if someone is under 18, you essentially have to check that everyone else is over 18, meaning millions of people are exposed to these systems. There is very little independent evidence on how well they work in non-ideal use cases, including in many real-world scenarios (e.g., in poor lighting). Most testing is done by the companies themselves, so we designed and completed our own privacy-preserving evaluations with in-person participants.

Jason: Both of those are fascinating. I use Twitter all the time, so I see Community Notes constantly. I’ve also seen the discourse around age verification on platforms like Roblox.

Since your work is so interdisciplinary, combining journalism with complex computational methods, what advice would you give to undergraduates looking to enter this field?

Madelyne: That’s a great question. My advice isn’t necessarily academic. I owe a lot of my current research direction to the fact that I took a few years off between undergrad and grad school to work full-time. I left undergrad with a bucket of interests but no real depth of understanding. I felt that I needed to spend time in the world to figure out which specific things I wanted to spend five or six years of my life digging into.

I did a post-baccalaureate at a natural history museum, then did a lot of media work. Through that, I realized I liked research, teaching, and working with journalists. Even during the “craziest” writer-editor interactions, I loved the behind-the-scenes work in newsrooms that readers and researchers often don’t see.

So, my advice is to take time off, if you’re considering graduate school but not sure about your next move. If you like media, spend time in a newsroom. See if technical research is something you want to combine with your other interests. You might decide that a PhD is right for you (and, if so, you’ll have a better sense of the problems you’re interested in working on). Or you might find that you’re happy pursuing a career outside of the academy – better to know this sooner rather than later.

Jason: Last question: what is the most interesting tidbit or surprise you’ve taken away from your research or experience?

Madelyne: On the research side, when we looked at automated fact-checking, we found a total lack of agreement on the definition of “misinformation.” A common workaround is “detection by proxy.” Instead of checking facts, a system might detect strong emotion or virality and use those as markers for whether something is true. As it turns out, that only works sometimes!

Jason Persaud is a Princeton University junior majoring in Operations Research & Financial Engineering (ORFE), pursuing minors in Finance and Machine Learning & Statistics. He works at the Center for Information Technology Policy as a Student Associate. Jason helped launch the Meet the Researcher series at CITP in the spring of 2025.

The post Meet the Researcher: Madelyne Xiao appeared first on CITP Blog.

title: Exploring post-quantum signature aggregation for EIP-8288
description:
by Manuel B. Santos (@manel1874) MultiVM Labs.
Motivation
Nowadays, the wallet ecosystem contains a plethora of features depending on different security models. These features require classical signatures to support threshold signing, key derivation or implementations that fit hardware signers. These properties are not generically present in post-quantum signature schemes; however, some proposed schemes do support them. Examples include Efficient Threshold ML-DSA, Threshold Raccoon, Falcon on Ledger Nano S+, and Raccoon-G HD wallets, which support public child-key derivation for watch-only wallets.
Ethereum is following a hash-based approach which generically lack the ability to directly support these different use-cases. Nonetheless, the conjunction between EIP-8141 and EIP-8288 provide a very agile path to support different signature schemes for wallets according to their needs. EIP-8141 proposes programmable account validation, while EIP-8288 proposes recursive STARK aggregation of signature and proof dependencies. Together, these drafts could let wallets choose their signing scheme while the network verifies a common proof.
In this post, we run five different signature schemes (Falcon-512, ML-DSA-44, FORS, Raccoon-128 and Raccoon-G) under a STARK proof and measure the proving, proof-size and verification costs of that approach.
Implementation
You can check this (experimental) implementation here. Falcon, ML-DSA and both Raccoon variants use leanVM’s experimental riscv-exploration branch, pinned to 06e5c9cd6981103786f9d0a17324241b559a50d3. Falcon reuses the implementation introduced by PR #490. On the other hand, FORS uses the Python leanISA guest at 575df819d9c857f38068cecf7b1640e0ce4bfb29. As per the current state, FORS achieve better performance with its specialised Keccak circuit.
Both RISC-V and leanISA based implementation follow the approach supported by leanVM summarized in the digram below.



Figure 1: leanVM proof possible flows (RISC-V left branch and leanISA right branch).

All four signature (Falcon, ML-DSA, FORS and Raccoon-128) verification mechanism fit inside one leanSTARK proof. However, Raccoon-G verification exceeds leanVM’s commitment cap: approximately 839 million witness words against a limit of 268 million. We explore next the approach taken to create a leanSTARK proof of one Raccoon-G signature verification mechanism.
Raccoon-G verification approach
The Raccoon-G verification mechanism follows the original Raccoon process described in Algorithm 3 of [PKPR24]. The expensive step is step 4 which can be summarized as:
where A is a 9\times 9 matrix of polynomials, z is a signature components, c_{poly} is its challenge polynomial, and T is a rounded and scaled public-key vector. The verifier, in step 5, computes the commitment vector w':= \text{Round}(y) + h, using the signature hint h, and then reconstructs  c'_{hash}=\mathsf{ChalHash}(w', \mu). Here \mu binds together the full public key and message and c_{hash} is the signature’s challenge digest.
Multi-STARK verification
As mentioned before, the whole signature verification process exceeds leamVM’s commitment cap, making it impossible to directly fit into one leanSTARK proof. Therefore, we focus on splitting the verification method into different leanSTARK proofs, which are then aggregated in a final leanSTARK.
Since the most expensive element is step 4 from [PKPR24], Alg. 3, we split the y computation \eqref{eq:full} in 5 sets of matrix rows and individually prove the rows relation in one leanSTARK. More specifically, for matrix row r given by
we create five proofs check rows: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7) and (8,8). Each leaf leanSTARK proof receives from the prover the whole signature \sigma and the proposed commitment vector w. Then, inside leanVM, each instance runs all steps from [PKPR24], Alg. 3 but step 4 and 5. Instead, it:
Reconstructs the two rows according to \eqref{eq:row} and get (w'_i, w'_j);
Checks equality with the corresponding supplied w rows, i.e., (w_i, w_j) == (w'_i, w'_j).
Moreover, to tie the leanSTARK proofs together, and to ensure different proofs do not use different witnesses pairs (\sigma, w), each proof computes a binding element D = H(\sigma, w) which needs to be passed to the verifier. Figure 2 summarizes this first process.



Figure 2: Matrix split structure and STARK proof elements.

After creating all 5 STARK proofs, these are aggregated together in a Merkle tree type fashion as depicted below in Figure 3. We combine the parts through leanVM’s native binary recursion circuits. So, for one signature, five fresh proofs occupy eight padded leaf slots, repeating the final proof for padding.
The receiver the is able to reconstruct all five expected outputs from its intended public-key/message pair and the prover’s untrusted D, then performs complete Tree::verify. This checks the root, ordered outputs and all remaining polynomial claims, without the need to see the signature \sigma and the intermediate commitment w.



Figure 3: Aggregation of multiple leanSTARK proofs into a final leanSTARK proof.

Experimental results
In this section, run some experiments to check the performance for proof generation and verification of alternative signatures under leanVM. We start by exploring single STARK proof generation for batched signatures and then check the impacts and limitations of having 10, 30, 70 and 100 distinct signatures for each of the five categories implemented (Falcon-512, ML-DSA-44, FORS, Raccoon-128 and Raccoon-G).
The machine used to host the experiments was an Apple M4 Pro with 24 GiB RAM. For each experiment we take the median of three fresh proofs after one warmup, in a fresh process and bars shown in the figures depict the full range. Also, we monitor the process-lifetime memory peak (RSS, Resident Set Size), including setup and warmup.
Direct batches
We start by checking how many signatures can be batched together in a single STARK. It verifies every signature and commits to the ordered keys and messages. As described in Figure 1 above, the verifier then needs to derive the expected commitment from its own intended public records, checks the approached program and proof parameters. In this section, we omit Raccoon-G because it requires more than one STARK proof for one signature proof verification.
Prover



Figure 4: Direct-batch proving costs under leanVM. Proof size (top left), proving time (top right), and peak prover memory (bottom) as the batch grows.

As we can see in the above figure, for the four alternative signatures analyzed, we were able to batch together 32 Falcon, 6 ML-DSA, 1 standard Raccoon and (at least) 100 FORS signatures. The cap on the first three schemes is related to the committed witness cap at 2^{28} words as depicted below in Figure 5.

Below, we measure complete direct-proof verification and exclude public claim derivation, setup and file reads.

Workload
Work per leaf




Falcon, RISC-V
10 signatures


ML-DSA, RISC-V
2 signatures


FORS, leanISA
5 signatures


Raccoon, RISC-V
1 signature


Raccoon-G, RISC-V
2 matrix rows




Prover

Its size therefore depends mainly on that root circuit and its proof parameters. Consequently, different signature algorithms require very different proving work while producing similarly sized roots.
On the other hand, FORS uses a different backend and recursive construction: leanISA verifier wrappers with the sumcheck reduction. Verifier
The verifier receives a receipt which contains the root STARK plus any auxiliary data required to verify it, such as Raccoon-G’s witness bindings or FORS’s remaining polynomial claims. So, the verifier performs three kinds of work which we presente in Figure 8 below:
Program setup (T_{\text{setup}}) means loading or compiling the approved programs and preparing verification tables and recursion circuits. FORS has substantially more preparation work in this implementation, explaining much of its high top-left curve in Figure 8.
Public processing (T_{\text{public processing}}) answers: “Does this proof concern the transactions I intend to accept?”
The verifier processes every original public-key/message pair, constructs the expected leaf commitments, and accounts for ordering and padding. For Raccoon-G, it constructs five part claims per signature using the same supplied D. This is the crux as a cryptographically valid proof for a different set of transactions would not authorize the intended transactions.
Proof verification (T_{\text{proof checks}}) answers: “Is that statement correctly proved?”
Figure 8 bottom-left panel includes the root STARK and all remaining verifier obligations. It is not just a check of the root transcript.
For RISC-V, complete Tree::verify checks the recursive proof and settles its remaining program, memory and circuit claims. For FORS, it checks the root STARK and evaluates the remaining reduced program claims. At 100 signatures, FORS has five such final evaluations.



Figure 8: Recursive STARK verification under leanVM. Top: complete verification including program setup (left) and with setup cached (right). Bottom: complete proof checks (left) and preparation of the public statement from all keys and messages (right).

Wallet infrastructure discussion
EIP-8288 opens the ability to integrate more complex cryptographic verification flows off-loading work from the EVM to off-chain proof computation. This makes it possible to integrate alternative signatures in wallet flows.
Memory constraints. If wallets generated their own leanSTARKs, proving would be a significant obstacle on browsers, phones and hardware signers. A conventional wasm32 build can address at most 4 GiB in one linear memory, and allocations can fail earlier when RAM is scarce. Memory64 increases the addressable range where supported, but provides no additional RAM. In Figure 4’s single-signature measurements, only Falcon-512 and FORS have native peak RSS below 4 GiB. These are plausible browser candidates, but larger batches or recursive proving can require much more memory.
A possible flow. The wallet signs locally and sends the transaction, public key and signature to an external untrusted aggregator (EUAgg), while (of course) its signing key stays on the device. The EUAgg then proves signature verification under leanVM and forwards the transactions and proof bundle to the mempool, where builders can aggregate them further. The network checks the final proof against the declared dependencies, while account validation requires the expected verifier, authorized key and signed transaction. Check Figure 9 for a diagram view of the flow.



Figure 9: Wallet infrastructure sketch with off-chain leanSTARK generation and aggregation.

This structure keeps proving off the wallet and lets users share proving costs. We note that EUAgg can delay or refuse service, but transaction authorization remains enforced by the account policy and proofs.
EIP-8288. This flow needs the draft’s generic STARK path to be completed and LEANSTARK_SCHEME is currently reserved and invalid in dependency frames. Also, AGGREGATED_VK and DEPS_HASH remain TBD. Integration must define the proof format and parameters, and bind each dependency to the signature-verification program, public key and transaction hash. The account’s validation logic must require that exact claim. Also, the draft sets MAX_LEANSTARK_DEPS_PER_WRAPPER=1, so a same-verifier batch that produces many individual proven dependencies therefore needs revised wrapper/admission limits and specified generic semantics. This would follow the same-verifier batching suggestion in the EIP-8288 discussion.

Motivation

Nowadays, the wallet ecosystem contains a plethora of features depending on different security models. These features require classical signatures to support threshold signing, key derivation or implementations that fit hardware signers. These properties are not generically present in post-quantum signature schemes; however, some proposed schemes do support them. Examples include Efficient Threshold ML-DSA, Threshold Raccoon, Falcon on Ledger Nano S+, and Raccoon-G HD wallets, which support public child-key derivation for watch-only wallets.

Ethereum is following a hash-based approach which generically lack the ability to directly support these different use-cases. Nonetheless, the conjunction between EIP-8141 and EIP-8288 provide a very agile path to support different signature schemes for wallets according to their needs. EIP-8141 proposes programmable account validation, while EIP-8288 proposes recursive STARK aggregation of signature and proof dependencies. Together, these drafts could let wallets choose their signing scheme while the network verifies a common proof.

In this post, we run five different signature schemes (Falcon-512, ML-DSA-44, FORS, Raccoon-128 and Raccoon-G) under a STARK proof and measure the proving, proof-size and verification costs of that approach.

Implementation

You can check this (experimental) implementation here. Falcon, ML-DSA and both Raccoon variants use leanVM’s experimental riscv-exploration branch, pinned to 06e5c9cd6981103786f9d0a17324241b559a50d3. Falcon reuses the implementation introduced by PR #490. On the other hand, FORS uses the Python leanISA guest at 575df819d9c857f38068cecf7b1640e0ce4bfb29. As per the current state, FORS achieve better performance with its specialised Keccak circuit.

Both RISC-V and leanISA based implementation follow the approach supported by leanVM summarized in the digram below.


Figure 1: leanVM proof possible flows (RISC-V left branch and leanISA right branch).

All four signature (Falcon, ML-DSA, FORS and Raccoon-128) verification mechanism fit inside one leanSTARK proof. However, Raccoon-G verification exceeds leanVM’s commitment cap: approximately 839 million witness words against a limit of 268 million. We explore next the approach taken to create a leanSTARK proof of one Raccoon-G signature verification mechanism.

Raccoon-G verification approach

The Raccoon-G verification mechanism follows the original Raccoon process described in Algorithm 3 of [PKPR24]. The expensive step is step 4 which can be summarized as:

y := A\cdot z - c_{poly}\cdot T, \tag{1}\label{eq:full}

where A is a 9\times 9 matrix of polynomials, z is a signature components, c_{poly} is its challenge polynomial, and T is a rounded and scaled public-key vector. The verifier, in step 5, computes the commitment vector w':= \text{Round}(y) + h, using the signature hint h, and then reconstructs c'_{hash}=\mathsf{ChalHash}(w', \mu). Here \mu binds together the full public key and message and c_{hash} is the signature’s challenge digest.

Multi-STARK verification

As mentioned before, the whole signature verification process exceeds leamVM’s commitment cap, making it impossible to directly fit into one leanSTARK proof. Therefore, we focus on splitting the verification method into different leanSTARK proofs, which are then aggregated in a final leanSTARK.

Since the most expensive element is step 4 from [PKPR24], Alg. 3, we split the y computation \eqref{eq:full} in 5 sets of matrix rows and individually prove the rows relation in one leanSTARK. More specifically, for matrix row r given by

y_r=\sum_{j=0}^{8}A_{r,j}\cdot z_j-c_{poly}\cdot T_r, \tag{2}\label{eq:row}

we create five proofs check rows: (0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,7) and (8,8). Each leaf leanSTARK proof receives from the prover the whole signature \sigma and the proposed commitment vector w. Then, inside leanVM, each instance runs all steps from [PKPR24], Alg. 3 but step 4 and 5. Instead, it:

  1. Reconstructs the two rows according to \eqref{eq:row} and get (w'_i, w'_j);
  2. Checks equality with the corresponding supplied w rows, i.e., (w_i, w_j) == (w'_i, w'_j).

Moreover, to tie the leanSTARK proofs together, and to ensure different proofs do not use different witnesses pairs (\sigma, w), each proof computes a binding element D = H(\sigma, w) which needs to be passed to the verifier. Figure 2 summarizes this first process.


Figure 2: Matrix split structure and STARK proof elements.

After creating all 5 STARK proofs, these are aggregated together in a Merkle tree type fashion as depicted below in Figure 3. We combine the parts through leanVM’s native binary recursion circuits. So, for one signature, five fresh proofs occupy eight padded leaf slots, repeating the final proof for padding.

The receiver the is able to reconstruct all five expected outputs from its intended public-key/message pair and the prover’s untrusted D, then performs complete Tree::verify. This checks the root, ordered outputs and all remaining polynomial claims, without the need to see the signature \sigma and the intermediate commitment w.


Figure 3: Aggregation of multiple leanSTARK proofs into a final leanSTARK proof.

Experimental results

In this section, run some experiments to check the performance for proof generation and verification of alternative signatures under leanVM. We start by exploring single STARK proof generation for batched signatures and then check the impacts and limitations of having 10, 30, 70 and 100 distinct signatures for each of the five categories implemented (Falcon-512, ML-DSA-44, FORS, Raccoon-128 and Raccoon-G).

The machine used to host the experiments was an Apple M4 Pro with 24 GiB RAM. For each experiment we take the median of three fresh proofs after one warmup, in a fresh process and bars shown in the figures depict the full range. Also, we monitor the process-lifetime memory peak (RSS, Resident Set Size), including setup and warmup.

We start by checking how many signatures can be batched together in a single STARK. It verifies every signature and commits to the ordered keys and messages. As described in Figure 1 above, the verifier then needs to derive the expected commitment from its own intended public records, checks the approached program and proof parameters. In this section, we omit Raccoon-G because it requires more than one STARK proof for one signature proof verification.

EIP-8288 opens the ability to integrate more complex cryptographic verification flows off-loading work from the EVM to off-chain proof computation. This makes it possible to integrate alternative signatures in wallet flows.

Ethereum (ETH USD) is trading near $1,800–$1,830 in mid-November 2026 after a sharp, multi-week decline that has tested many holders’ resolve. Despite the recent weakness and broader market pressure, an over-the-top bullish scenario still leaves room for a powerful recovery by January 1, 2027.

The landmark catalyst unlocking this extreme upside is a highly unlikely but not impossible structural breakthrough in Ethereum’s role as the settlement layer for tokenized real-world assets and institutional finance.

(SOURCE: Meta AI Predicts ETH to Explode)

In this hypothetical, a coordinated wave of major traditional financial institutions and asset managers formally designates Ethereum (and its leading Layer-2 networks) as the primary infrastructure for large-scale tokenized securities, funds, and on-chain settlement.

Combined with accelerated progress on scalability upgrades and clearer regulatory pathways, this creates sustained structural demand for ETH as both gas and a core collateral asset, driving a sharp re-rating.

ETH USD Technical Analysis

Market Cap

ETH has broken lower from levels above $2,000 and is now consolidating in the $1,800 region after testing support near $1,750–$1,780. The recent decline has produced a series of lower highs, with immediate resistance clustered around $1,900–$2,000 and a more significant supply zone near the prior local highs.

On the downside, the $1,700–$1,750 area represents the next key demand zone. Momentum indicators have cooled substantially after the sell-off, leaving the asset oversold on intermediate timeframes and creating conditions that have historically preceded sharp relief rallies once forced selling exhausts.

In a standard recovery, a sustained weekly close back above $2,000 would be an important first confirmation that the corrective phase is ending. Under the extreme institutional-tokenization catalyst outlined above, those intermediate levels would be cleared rapidly, allowing measured-move extensions and multi-cycle projections from the current base to support a far more aggressive upside trajectory.

While the past few weeks have been unambiguously difficult and have pushed many investors into a defensive posture, Ethereum has repeatedly shown it can recover from deep drawdowns when structural demand returns.

Ongoing technical development, institutional product infrastructure, and the theoretical potential for a major shift in real-world asset settlement keep the door open for a powerful rebound.
